Given the targets of amivantamab, we evaluated the relationship between EGFR expression and antitumor immunity. We evaluated EGFR expression with IHC (Fig. S4A), which was then classified into 4 categories (0-3 +) based on a previous report (Fig. 3A). In the entire cohort, 34% (13/38) of the tumors were classified as EGFR <= 1 + and 66% (25/38) were EGFR >= 2 + (Fig. 3A). As previously reported, the majority of the EGFR-mutant tumors highly expressed EGFR (85%, 11/13). However, more than half of EGFR-WT tumors also expressed high levels of EGFR (59%, 13/22) (Fig. 3B). There was a trend toward an association between EGFR mutation and EGFR expression, although not statistically significant (Fisher's exact test: P = 0.150).

We next compared the immune microenvironment and immune cell phenotypes according to EGFR expression. As a result, infiltration of CD8+ T cells and DCs was significantly reduced in EGFR >= 2 + tumors (Fig. S4B and C). In contrast, the ratio of CD8+ T cells to eTregs, as well as the activation status of CD8+ T cells, DCs, and eTregs, was comparable irrespective of EGFR expression levels (Fig. S4D-I). We further analyzed the relationship between EGFR expression and amivantamab-mediated immune activation. Amivantamab increased PD-1 expression and cytokine production in CD8+ TILs from EGFR >= 2 + tumors, whereas these effects were limited in EGFR <= 1 + tumors (Fig. 3C-E). Similarly, tumor-infiltrating DC maturation was significantly promoted by amivantamab in EGFR >= 2 + tumors but remained limited in EGFR <= 1 + tumors (Fig. S4J and K). In contrast, tumor-infiltrating eTregs were unaffected by amivantamab in EGFR >= 2 + tumors (Fig. S4L and M). These findings suggest that high EGFR expression is associated with an immunosuppressive TME, but amivantamab can promote immune activation in such a TME.

Similar to EGFR, we also examined MET, another target of amivantamab, by classifying its expression in tumors into four categories (0-3 +) based on the previous report. In the entire cohort, MET was highly expressed (2 + or 3 +) in half of the cases (19/38) (Fig. 3F and Fig. S5A). The comparison of immune features between MET >= 2 + and MET <= 1 + tumors revealed no significant differences in CD8+ T-cell or DC infiltration (Fig. S5B and C) and in the CD8+ T cell to eTreg ratio (Fig. S5D). In addition, the activation status of CD8+ T cells, DCs, and eTregs were also comparable between the two groups (Fig. S5E-I). However, in MET >= 2 + tumors, amivantamab increased PD-1 expression and cytokine production in CD8+ TILs, whereas such effects were limited in MET <= 1 + tumors (Fig. 3G-I). Tumor-infiltrating DC maturation tended to be promoted by amivantamab regardless of MET expression (Fig. S5J and K), while tumor-infiltrating eTregs remained unchanged MET >= 2 + tumors (Fig. S5L and M). Taken together, these findings suggest that, similar to EGFR, MET expression can be associated with immune-activating effects of amivantamab.

We also stratified tumors using a more stringent 3 + cut-off for EGFR and MET expression (0-2 + vs. 3 +). As a result, amivantamab treatment significantly increased PD-1 expression and cytokine production in CD8+ TILs from EGFR 3 + tumors, whereas cytokine production was also induced in EGFR 0-2 + tumors (Fig. S6A-C), suggesting that a certain level of EGFR expression may be sufficient to support amivantamab-mediated immune activation. Conversely, amivantamab did not induce a significant increase in PD-1 expression or cytokine production in MET 3 + tumors (n = 5) (Fig. S6D-F), which may be due to the limited number of samples.

Given the individual importance of EGFR and MET expression in amivantamab-mediated immune activation, we next analyzed their combined association. The cohort was divided into four groups based on EGFR and MET expression as described in Fig. 4A, which exhibited a significant association between EGFR and MET expression levels (Fisher's exact test: P = 0.038). Although EGFR and MET expression were positively correlated, 32% (12/38) of the tumors exhibited EGFR or MET expression scored as >= 2 + (Fig. 4A). We subsequently divided the tumors into two groups according to EGFR and MET expression levels (Group I: both <= 1 + ; Group II: either >= 2 +) (Fig. 4A), and compared their immune microenvironment and immune cell phenotypes. The results revealed that tumors in group II exhibited a trend toward lower CD8+ T-cell infiltration (Fig. S7A) and significantly reduced DC infiltration (Fig. S7B). In contrast, the CD8+ T cell to eTreg ratio and the activation status of immune cells were comparable between the two groups (Fig. S7C-H). We also examined the association of EGFR and MET expression with the immune-activating effects of amivantamab. In group II tumors, amivantamab increased PD-1 expression and cytokine production in CD8+ TILs. In contrast, in group I tumors, amivantamab-induced CD8+ TIL activation was limited (Fig. 4B-D). Similarly, tumor-infiltrating DC maturation was promoted by amivantamab in group II tumors, but not in group I tumors (Fig. S7I and J). Tumor-infiltrating eTregs were unaffected by amivantamab in group II tumors (Fig. S7K and L). Collectively, these findings indicate that high expression of EGFR or MET is important for amivantamab-induced immune responses.

We further hypothesized that EGFR and MET expression might influence the efficacy of amivantamab even in EGFR-WT tumors. EGFR-mutant and EGFR-WT tumors were each stratified into four groups based on EGFR and MET expression as described in Fig. 5A, and 72.7% (16/22) tumors exhibited >= 2 + expression of either EGFR or MET even among EGFR-WT tumors (Fig. 5A). No significant correlation was observed between EGFR mutation status and EGFR or MET expression (Fisher's exact test: P = 0.680). Then, using the same EGFR and MET expression criteria, EGFR-WT tumors were further divided into group I (both <= 1 +) and group II (either >= 2 +) (Fig. 5A). We then examined the association of EGFR and MET expression with the immune-activating effects of amivantamab in EGFR-WT tumors. Even in group II tumors with EGFR-WT, amivantamab significantly increased PD-1 expression and cytokine production in CD8+ TILs (Fig. 5B-D). A trend toward amivantamab-induced DC maturation was observed only in group II, but not in group I (Fig. S7A and B). In contrast, amivantamab did not induce significant changes in tumor-infiltrating eTregs in either group (Fig. S8C and D). These findings suggest that even EGFR-WT tumors, the presence of EGFR or MET expression can allow amivantamab to promote immune responses.
Amivantamab activates immune responses in tumors with EGFR phosphorylation

Considering the importance of EGFR and MET signaling in antitumor immunity, We evaluated the relationship between EGFR phosphorylation (pEGFR) (Fig S9A) and the immunomodulatory effects of amivantamab. In our cohort, 45% (17/38) of the tumors exhibited pEGFR expression. We stratified the cohort according to pEGFR into positive and negative groups, which was evaluated using a previous method. As previously reported, the majority of the EGFR-mutant tumors exhibited pEGFR, with a significant trend toward an association between EGFR mutation and pEGFR (Fisher's exact test: P = 0.0425) (Fig. S9B). Although a previous report suggested that EGFR expression and phosphorylation do not necessarily correlate, a significant correlation was observed in our cohort (Fisher's exact test: P = 0.0151) (Fig. S9B). We further analyzed the relationship between pEGFR and amivantamab-mediated immune activation. As a result, amivantamab increased PD-1 expression and cytokine production in CD8+ TILs from pEGFR-positive tumors, whereas it increased only TNFalpha production in CD8+ TILs from pEGFR-negative tumors (Fig. S9C-E). Tumor-infiltrating DC maturation also tended to be promoted by amivantamab in pEGFR-positive tumors (Fig. S9F and G). In contrast, tumor-infiltrating eTregs were unaffected by amivantamab regardless of pEGFR status (Fig. S9H and I). These results support the importance of EGFR signaling in regulating immune responses. Similar to pEGFR, we evaluated the relationship between MET phosphorylation (pMET) (Fig. S10A) and the immunomodulatory effects of amivantamab. Only 13% (5/38) of the cases were positive for pMET, which was not significantly correlated with total MET expression (Fig. S10B). Immune activation induced by amivantamab was not observed in pMET-positive tumors (n = 5) (Fig. S10C-I), which may be attributable to the limited sample size.
Discussion

EGFR-mutant NSCLCs are characterized by the immunosuppressive TME and poor responses to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). EGFR mutations induce ligand-independent phosphorylation of RTK and activate EGFR signaling pathways, which contribute not only to cancer cell proliferation but also to the establishment of immunosuppressive TME. Specifically, EGFR activation regulates chemokine production, leading to reduced infiltration of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells while promoting the recruitment of Tregs. This pathway also increases tumor-promoting cytokines and EGFR ligands, suppressing CD8+ T-cell function and DC maturation while enhancing the immunosuppressive activity of Tregs and tumor-associated macrophages. Consistently, in our cohort, EGFR-mutant tumors exhibited reduced infiltration of CD8+ T cells and DCs, reinforcing the concept of the immunosuppressive TME in these tumors. As with EGFR, MET has also been reported to suppress antitumor immune responses. Therefore, blockade of the EGFR and MET pathways could potentially counteract this immunosuppressive TME. Consistently, amivantamab, a bispecific antibody targeting both EGFR and MET, has demonstrated a tail plateau pattern in clinical responses, which suggests that amivantamab can activate antitumor immunity. However, amivantamab-induced immune activation has been demonstrated only in vitro and in mouse models, with no direct evidence from human clinical specimens. In this study, we provide the first direct evidence from ex vivo fresh TIL assays using human NSCLC clinical specimens that amivantamab can activate antitumor immune responses, particularly through T-cell-mediated responses.

Although the mechanisms underlying amivantamab-induced immune activation remain incompletely understood, studies of other receptor-targeting antibodies may offer relevant insights. Human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-targeted antibodies, which are reported to show clinical responses when combined with ICIs for HER2-positive gastric cancer, have been shown to alleviate immune suppression. The immunomodulatory effects are reportedly mediated by inhibition of HER2 signaling and Fc-dependent mechanisms, including ADCC and ADCP activity. Similarly, because both EGFR and MET signaling pathways are involved in immune suppression, their blockade by amivantamab may relieve immune suppression and promote immune activation. Consistently, in our cohort, amivantamab-induced immune activation correlated with EGFR phosphorylation status. In addition, amivantamab is engineered to enhance ADCC and ADCP activity through reduced fucosylation, and we also observed DC maturation following amivantamab treatment although its correlation with EGFR or MET expression was less clear than that observed for T cells. Because tumor-infiltrating natural killer (NK) cells are generally small, their potential contribution was not evaluated in our cohort, highlighting the need for further investigation.

Although amivantamab is currently approved only for EGFR-mutant NSCLC, previous reports have suggested efficacy in EGFR-WT tumors. Consistently, we observed that amivantamab promoted TIL activation in tumors with high EGFR or MET expression, regardless of mutation status. This finding is aligned with its pharmacological mechanism and underscores the potential of EGFR/MET expression as biomarkers for amivantamab-induced antitumor immunity. Indeed, several ongoing clinical trials are already including EGFR-WT cohorts, and our results support such trial designs. Importantly, these findings suggest that tumors with high EGFR/MET expression may benefit from amivantamab even without EGFR mutations.

From a methodological perspective, mouse models frequently fail to predict human clinical outcomes, and peripheral blood-based assays cannot recapitulate the chronic antigen exposure and suppressive cues that shape TIL function in the TME. In contrast, our fresh TIL assay preserves the viability of tumor and immune cells, enabling real-time assessment of therapeutic antibody activity within a physiologically relevant context. Unlike assays relying on TIL expansion, organoid generation, or cryopreservation, our approach is very simple, minimizing artifacts and reflecting in vivo conditions more faithfully. Voabil et al. also developed a similar tumor fragment platform, showing the advantages. This approach not only provides a more faithful reflection of the in vivo TME but also holds broader implications for drug development. Moreover, with further development, this approach could evolve into a patient-specific tool, enabling clinicians to project therapeutic responses to treatment.

In summary, this study provides the first ex vivo human evidence that amivantamab activates TILs together with the unique strengths of our fresh TIL assay. These effects extended beyond EGFR-mutant tumors to EGFR-WT tumors with high EGFR or MET expression, underscoring the potential of EGFR/MET expression as biomarkers for amivantamab-induced antitumor immunity. Further basic and translational research is warranted to validate these findings and guide future clinical applications.

passages.text: Prediction of depressive episodes based on clinical features, cognitive characteristics, inflammation-related proteins, and EEG data

The absence of clinically validated biomarkers and objective diagnostic protocols hinders the accurate and effective diagnosis of depression. Although machine learning has been increasingly explored in psychiatric diagnosis, there remains a pressing need to develop a reliable tool that integrates multimodal data:such as clinical features, cognitive functions, electroencephalographic microstates, and inflammation-associated proteins:to improve diagnostic accuracy and objectivity. One hundred and fifteen patients with depression and 66 healthy controls were included in this study, and data on their clinical characteristics, cognitive function, electroencephalographic microstates, and serum inflammation-related proteins were collected. The baseline depression group was followed up after 4 weeks of clinical treatment, with 56 participants completing the follow-up survey, which mirrored the baseline survey. The depression baseline and healthy control groups were designated as the training set, while the follow-up and healthy control groups served as the validation set. Six classical machine learning algorithms:Decision Tree, Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, k-Nearest Neighbor, and Support Vector Machine:were employed to train the diagnostic prediction model using the training set. The model was then validated with the validation set to identify the optimal depression diagnostic prediction model. The results of the study showed significant differences in clinical characteristics, cognitive function, EEG microstates, and serum levels of inflammation-related proteins in patients with major depressive disorder compared with healthy controls. In the model evaluation, the k-nearest neighbor model performed the best, with an accuracy of 95.08% for multimodal diagnosis, an F1 score of 0.9545, and an AUC value of 0.9969. In order of feature importance were IL-8, IL-18, ISI, MMP-8, CD40, CASP-8, visuospatial/constructional, and mean duration of EEG microstate D. A multimodal, multi-indicator model (incorporating L-8, IL-18, ISI, MMP-8, CD40, CASP-8, visuospatial/constructional abilities, and mean duration of EEG microstate D) has the potential to enhance the accuracy and objectivity of clinical depression diagnoses.
Background

Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) is a globally prevalent mental disorder affecting approximately 280 million people worldwide. By 2030, MDD will be the leading contributor to the global burden of disease. The main clinical features of depression include loss of pleasure, diminished interest, depressed mood, decreased energy, cognitive dysfunction, and vegetative symptoms such as changes in sleep, appetite, and weight. However, MDD relies heavily on patient interviews and questionnaire assessments for diagnosis and treatment. Specific biomarkers, on the other hand, complement the diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of depression.

With the application of nonlinear feature extraction and cluster analysis, EEG with high temporal resolution characteristics has attracted much attention. Compared with CT and MRI techniques, it is simple and easy to perform with no radiation or noise. It is highly accepted by the subjects, which has good prospects for future diagnostic applications. The EEG observes abnormalities in functional connectivity and neural activity, which are characteristic brain network alterations present in depressed patients. In resting-state EEG analysis, a stable topographic pattern persists for approximately 80-120 milliseconds, and this transiently stable state is referred to as an EEG microstate. According to previous studies, EEG microstates are typically classified into four canonical paradigms:A, B, C, and D:corresponding to the auditory, visual, cognitive control, and dorsal attention networks, respectively. As a highly reliable analytical method, resting-state EEG microstates often reflect distributed neural network information processing states and serve as a valuable tool for assessing brain network activity. Therefore, resting-state EEG microstates may be potential biomarkers to assist in the diagnosis and prognosis of treatment efficacy in MDD.

Hypotheses of the biological mechanisms of MDD involve the monoamine neurotransmitter hypothesis, alterations in the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, mechanisms of chronic inflammatory action, neuroplasticity, and neurogenesis. Of these, chronic inflammatory mechanisms are more likely to have significant clinical value in aiding the diagnostic and therapeutic targeting of MDD. There is a strong correlation between high levels of inflammatory markers and depressive episodes. A large cross-sectional study of over 6000 participants found that men with current or past depressive episodes were more likely to exhibit elevated CRP levels compared to healthy controls. Further studies found that elevated serum IL-1beta and IL-18, as well as upregulation of NLRP3 inflammatory vesicles and caspase-1 enzymes, were also detected in depressed patients. A prospective cohort study that annually assessed inflammatory markers and depressive symptoms in children between the ages of 9 and 18 years found that individuals with higher plasma levels of IL-6 at age 9 years had a significantly increased risk of developing depression at age 18 years. The results of a Meta-analysis suggested that peripheral levels of IL-6, TNF-alpha, IL-10, soluble IL-2R, C-C chemokine ligand 2, IL-13, IL-18, IL-12, IL-1 receptor antagonist, and soluble TNFR2 were elevated in patients with depression compared to the general population, whereas interferon-gamma levels were lower in depressed patients. The results of another meta-analysis found that antidepressant treatment was able to reduce IL-6 levels, and that persistently elevated levels of TNF-alpha were associated with treatment resistance. The evidence from the above studies demonstrates the great potential of inflammation-related proteins in the diagnosis and treatment prediction of MDD.

Machine learning is a computational technique for analyzing large multidimensional complex data with nonlinear relationships by identifying patterns of interaction between multiple variables. In recent years, this technology has been increasingly utilized in psychiatry to enhance the precision and optimization of disease diagnosis and treatment. A Random Forest-based diagnostic prediction model was developed using structural and resting-state functional MRI data from 260 depressed patients and 127 healthy controls, achieving an AUC of 0.802 in differentiating anxious from non-anxious depression through 10-fold cross-validation. Additionally, psychological assessment data from 149 patients with refractory depression across multiple centers were collected at baseline and at follow-ups in January and March to develop a Random Forest model for predicting medication effects, achieving accuracies of 68.53 and 66.26% for January and March, respectively. Using data from the NHANES 2013-2014 cycle (N = 5372), Thien Vu et al. implemented an 80/20 train-test split and compared six machine-learning approaches, finding that XGBoost outperformed the other models (AUC = 0.69), with the poverty-income ratio identified as the dominant predictive feature.

However, the above studies have a single dimension and poor accuracy of validation after modeling. In fact, predictive models that incorporate multiple data types tend to outperform models with a single data type. Therefore, this study aims to integrate multidimensional data, including clinical symptoms, cognitive features, EEG microstates, and peripheral circulating inflammatory proteins, utilizing machine learning techniques to identify key features and develop a predictive model for disease diagnosis. Model performance is optimized through training and validation with post-treatment data, aiming to identify high-quality biomarkers to assist in the accurate diagnosis of MDD.
Methods
Overview of participant selection and data collection

We informed all participants and their guardians in detail and signed a formal informed consent form before enrollment. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Guangji Hospital, Suzhou, China (Ethics Approval Number: 2020008).
Sample size estimation

Sample size calculation formula for hypothesis testing of two-population exposure rates using a case-control study design:Where n denotes the sample size, the Type I error alpha (two-tailed) is 0.05, the power (1-beta) is 0.90, the exposure ratio p0 in the control group is 0.05, and the exposure ratio p1 in the case group is 0.30. The mean exposure ratio for both groups is 0.18. Calculating the minimum sample size for a single group yields 47 cases.
Inclusion criteria for the depression group

(1) Diagnosis confirmed by two attending or senior psychiatric clinicians using the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-5 Axis I Disorders (SCID), with participants meeting DSM-5 criteria for MDD. (2) Symptom severity was assessed using the Hamilton Depression Scale (HAMD-24) and Hamilton Anxiety Scale (HAMA-17). (3) Right-handed individuals aged 18-60 years. (4) Completion of at least nine years of formal education. (5) Patients and their guardians fully understand the study details and voluntarily provide written informed consent.
Inclusion criteria for the healthy control group

(1) Age- and sex-matched individuals recruited from the same region as the depressed patients. (2) Assessed by a psychiatrist, with SCID-5 confirming no current or past Axis I psychiatric disorders. (3) Completion of at least nine years of compulsory education. (4) No family history of psychiatric disorders. (5) Participants fully understand the study details and voluntarily provide written informed consent.
Exclusion criteria

(1) History of convulsion-free Modified Electroconvulsive Therapy (MECT) within six months prior to enrollment. (2) Significant abnormalities in laboratory tests (e.g., liver and kidney function) or imaging examinations (e.g., cranial CT) before enrollment. (3) Diagnosis of other psychiatric disorders, such as intellectual disability. (4) Diagnosis of neurological disorders, including epilepsy, traumatic brain injury, or multiple sclerosis. (5) Dependence on or abuse of addictive substances (e.g., alcohol). (6) Pregnancy or lactation. (7) Presence of metallic implants or other implanted medical devices. (8) Use of anti-inflammatory or hormonal medications.

This study collected comprehensive data, including demographic information, clinical characteristics, cognitive function assessments, electroencephalographic (EEG) microstate data, and fasting serum samples, from 115 patients with depression at baseline and 66 healthy controls. Among them, 56 depressed patients who completed four weeks of antidepressant treatment underwent follow-up assessments, including repeated evaluations of clinical characteristics, cognitive function, EEG microstates, and fasting serum analysis. All enrolled patients with depression received monoamine-based antidepressant therapy, with specific medication regimens determined by the attending physician based on individual clinical presentations. During data collection, 10 patients with depression were excluded: two developed manic symptoms, three were unable to complete baseline EEG, two failed to complete the baseline cognitive assessment, and one had unsuccessful baseline serum collection. Additionally, four healthy control participants were excluded: one due to a high HAMD score, two for incomplete EEG recordings, and one whose EEG data were not suitable for analysis.
Clinical assessments

Clinical assessment was performed by an experienced psychiatrist. General demographic information about the subjects was collected, including gender, age, years of education, duration of illness, number of depressive episodes, and age at first episode. The Hamilton Depression Scale (HAMD-24), Hamilton Anxiety Scale (HAMA), Insomnia Severity Index Scale (ISI), and Depression-Related Anhedonia Scale (DARS) were used to assess the degree of depression, anxiety, insomnia, and pleasure deficit.
Cognitive function assessment

Cognitive abilities in both the depressed group and healthy controls were assessed using the Repeatable Battery for the Assessment of Neuropsychological Status (RBANS). The RBANS includes 12 subtests that are categorized into five neuropsychological domains: Immediate Memory, Visuospatial/Constructional, Language, Attention, and Delayed Memory. The RBANS scores are reported as standardized scores, allowing for comparison of cognitive performance both across subjects and over time within the same subject.
Collection and processing of blood sample

Five milliliters of fasting venous blood were collected from the elbow without anticoagulants before 8:00 a.m. for both depressed patients and healthy control participants. Subsequently, the blood samples were placed in a centrifuge and centrifuged at 3000 rpm for 10 min. The supernatant (serum) was accurately extracted using a pipette and transferred to a 500 microl EP tube. After dispensing, the serum samples were properly stored in a cryogenic refrigerator at -80 degrees Celsius for subsequent testing. The same procedure was followed for the collection and processing of the serum from the follow-up depressed patients.

Thirty-one inflammation-associated proteins including were analyzed in serum using a Luminex multiplexed liquid microarray assay: Thirty-one inflammation-associated proteins including nine anti-inflammatory proteins (BMP-2, BMP-9, BMP-10, Dkk1, HGF, IL-10, IL-13, IL-27, Park-7/Dj-1), 12 pro-inflammatory proteins (ARRIL/TNFSF-13, BAFF/ TNFSF-13B, IL-7, IL-8/CXCL8, IL-15, IL-18/IL1F4, MMP-2, MMP-7, MMP-10, RAGE/AGER, S100A9, VCAM1/CD106) and 10 other inflammation-related proteins (Cytatin.C, Endocan/ESM-1, ErbB-3/Her-3, Ferritin, IGFprp1/IGFBP7, PDGF-BB, PDGF-CC, PDGF-DD, Tenascin.C, uPAR). In addition, four pro-inflammatory proteins (CASP-8, CD40, MMP-8, uPA) and one anti-inflammatory protein (TGF-alpha) were measured in serum using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA).
EEG data acquisition and preprocessing

Subjects were seated in a comfortable position in an electrically shielded room, and data were acquired using an EGI 256-lead EEG acquisition system (EGI System 400; Electrical Geodesic Inc.) with a sampling rate of 1000 Hz and Cz as the reference electrode. Ensure that the scalp resistance is lower than 50 kOmega, and set the low-frequency filtering to 1 Hz and the high-frequency filtering to 80 Hz. 5-minute resting-state EEGs were acquired in the eyes-open and eyes-closed states, respectively.

Participants' EEG data were preprocessed using the HAPPE toolbox in MATLAB (version 2022b; MathWorks, Inc.), which implements a standardized, automated pipeline including line noise removal and artifact rejection via Wavelet-Thresholding and ICA with MARA. Following this automated preprocessing (0.5-45 Hz bandwidth), the data underwent a visual quality check to verify signal integrity and technical quality, ensuring that no gross artifacts remained. This step did not involve manual rejection of specific epochs. Subsequently, the EEG data were further bandpass filtered to 2-20 Hz specifically for microstate analysis. Global field power (GFP) was used to quantify the overall picture of potential changes at all electrodes, thus reflecting real-time changes in the strength of the brain's electric field. The AAHC algorithm was used to determine the four optimal microstate topographies. The microstate maps were sorted and labeled to maximize their spatial correlation with the canonical normative reference maps, utilizing the templates provided in the MicrostateAnalysis plugin (v1.2). This step ensures the comparability of our microstate classes (A-D) with existing literature. The 4-map solution explained a substantial proportion of the global variance in the EEG data (Mean Global Explained Variance [GEV]: 75.0% for the MDD group and 78.2% for the HC group), confirming that the four canonical maps sufficiently captured the topographic dynamics of the study population.

Subsequently, the clustering results were rearranged according to a standard microstate template map. This step involves clustering the data for all subjects to create a set of topographic maps representing the brain topology of all participants. Ultimately, a new dataset was generated that included the individual temporal parameters of the microstates for subsequent statistical analysis.
Statistical analysis

We compared the demographics, clinical characteristics, cognitive function, EEG microstates, and serum levels of inflammation-related proteins between individuals with MDD and HC. Data are presented as mean +- standard deviation (S.D.) for continuous variables or as percentage frequency (%) for categorical variables. The Shapiro-Wilk test was used to assess normality. T-tests and analysis of variance (ANOVA) were applied to normally distributed variables, while the chi-square test was used for categorical variables. All analyses were conducted using IBM SPSS Statistics 26 and R version 4.2.3. Statistical significance was defined as P < 0.05, with all tests being two-tailed. In addition, multiple testing was adjusted with the Bonferroni correction (0.05/N). N denotes the number of multiple corrections.
Machine learning models for MDD diagnosis prediction

To objectively differentiate between MDD and HC, we developed a new diagnostic model by integrating clinical characteristics, cognitive function assessments, biomarkers from serum inflammation-related proteins, and electrophysiological data. The model's performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, with F1 scores and accuracies derived from 10-fold cross-validation to evaluate its predictive validity. Six classical machine learning algorithms:Decision Tree (DT), K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LGBM), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGB), and Random Forest (RF):were compared to identify the optimal model for MDD diagnosis prediction. Once the optimal MDD diagnostic model was selected, feature contributions to the predictions were analyzed using Shapley Additive explanations (SHAP) for transparent and interpretable decision-making. SHAP, based on Shapley value theory from cooperative game theory, assigns an influence score to each feature, representing its importance in model predictions. SHAP visual analytics is widely applied in various machine learning contexts, whether for classification or regression tasks, and provides comprehensive explanations of feature contributions.

Overview of adjunctive depression diagnosis.

The study ultimately recruited 181 participants, including 115 individuals with major depressive disorder (MDD) and 66 age- and sex-matched healthy controls (HC). The enrolled MDD participants were followed up after four weeks of treatment, with 56 completing the follow-up. Clinical characteristics and cognitive function were assessed, serum levels of inflammation-related proteins were measured, and electroencephalography was refined for the baseline group, follow-up group, and HC group. The baseline and HC groups were designated as the training set, while the follow-up and HC groups formed the validation set. Six machine learning algorithms (DT, RF, LightBGM, XGBoost, kNN, and SVM) were applied to the training set to develop a predictive model for depression diagnosis. Ten-fold cross-validation was performed to enhance model stability, and the validation set was used to identify the optimal model and its parameters.

The results showed that MDD's log-transformed (taking ln values) MMP-2, MMP-7, MMP-10, Ferritin, PDGF-BB, IL-7, IL-15, IL-8/CXCL8, Tenascin.C, uPAR, ARRIL/TNFSF-13, BMP-2, BMP-10, Endocan/ESM-1, RAGE/AGER, S100A9, VCAM1/CD106, and CASP-8 levels were significantly lower than those of the HC (P < 0.05) (Table 3 and Fig. 1). The ln-transformed levels of PDGF-CC, BAFF/TNFSF13B, IGFPrp1/IGFBP7, BMP-9, CD40, IL-18/IL1F4, TGF-alpha, and MMP-8 were significantly higher in MDD than in the HC (P < 0.05) (Table 3 and Fig. 2).
A novel predictive model for the diagnosis of depression

We selected the metrics that showed significant differences between the MDD and HC groups at baseline as features for the depression diagnostic training model. The data were grouped based on the "Grouping" column, and for each variable, the proportion of missing values within each group was calculated separately. Variables with more than 30% missing values in any group were excluded from the dataset. For the remaining variables, different imputation strategies were applied: random forest imputation (MissForest) was used for numerical variables, and the mode (plurality) method was used for categorical variables.

The features to be selected were included in the least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator Regression (Lasso) regression for feature selection. This study used 5-fold cross-validation to select the optimal lambda value. The analysis showed that the optimal lambda-value was 0.0003574076, and the final screened features were: four clinical symptom features (ISI, PH, SA, SE), two cognitive function features (Visuospatial/Constructional, Attention), four EEG microstate features (dur.d, occ.c, cov.b, cov.d) and ten inflammation-related protein indicators (MMP-2, IL-15, IL-7, TNFSF-13B, BMP-9, IL-8, IL-18, CASP-8, CD40, MMP-8)(Fig. 3a and b). We further refined the 20 features selected through Lasso regression by considering the small-sample, multidimensional characteristics of this study. The most significant clinical features, cognitive indicators, and EEG microstates were retained, along with the top five inflammation-related proteins. The final set of features included ISI, Visuospatial, dur.d, IL-8, IL-18, CASP-8, CD40, and MMP-8.

The AUC, accuracy, and F1 scores were used to evaluate the performance of each machine-learning model. The results indicated that the XGB model achieved the highest AUC value of 1, followed by LGBM, RF, SVM, KNN, and DT in descending order (Fig. 3c). All six models demonstrated an accuracy above 96%, with F1 scores exceeding 95%. In summary, the XGB model outperformed the others in the training set. The results of machine learning model training revealed that the KNN model achieved the highest AUC value of 0.9969, followed by the SVM, LGBM, RF, and DT models in that order (Fig. 3d). The KNN model also achieved the highest F1 score (95.08%) and the highest accuracy (95.45%). In summary, the KNN model demonstrated the best performance in the validation set.

This study further demonstrates the interpretability of the KNN model results. As shown in the SHAP importance bar chart, the most important feature was IL-8, followed by IL-18, ISI score, MMP-8, CD40, CASP-8, Visuospatial/Constructional, and the mean duration of EEG microstate D (Fig. 3e). The SHAP honeycomb chart provides a global view of the influence of each feature (Fig. 3f). Additionally, the SHAP waterfall chart illustrates the cumulative contribution of each feature from baseline to prediction (Fig. 3g). To quantify the incremental predictive value of inflammation-related proteins, we performed ablation analyses by systematically excluding all inflammatory protein features (CD40, IL-8, IL-18, CASP-8, and MMP-8) from the full model. Removal of these variables led to a marked deterioration in model performance, with the macro F1 score declining from 95.08% to 60.66% (Delta = -0.3442; P < 0.001, DeLong test) and the AUC decreasing from 0.9969 to 0.7173 (Delta = -0.2796; P < 0.001, DeLong test). These pronounced reductions indicate that inflammation-related protein markers contribute critical and non-redundant information to the predictive architecture of the model and are essential for accurate depression classification.
Discussion

In this study, a diagnostic prediction model was developed using six classical machine learning methods (DT, RF, XGB, LGBM, KNN, and SVM) based on significant differences in clinical features, cognitive functions, EEG microstates, and serum levels of inflammation-related proteins between MDD and HC. For the first time, EEG microstates were integrated with clinical features, cognitive indicators, and serum inflammatory protein levels to predict depression diagnosis using machine learning algorithms. The validation results demonstrated that the KNN model performed optimally, achieving a diagnostic accuracy of 95.08%, an F1 score of 0.9545, and an AUC of 0.9969. According to the SHAP values, the most important features in the model were IL-8, IL-18, ISI, MMP-8, CD40, CASP-8, Visuospatial/Constructional, and the mean duration of EEG microstate D. Additionally, the model based on the multidimensional multi-indicator approach showed higher accuracy in distinguishing depressed from non-depressed groups compared to a unidimensional multi-indicator combination.

Increasing evidence suggests that abnormalities in immunoinflammatory pathways and the activation of cell-mediated immunity are critical pathophysiological mechanisms in the development of depression. Peripheral immune dysfunction, characterized by low-grade inflammation, may influence brain function by allowing inflammation-associated proteins to cross the blood-brain barrier. Previous studies have indicated that pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IL-18, contribute to depressive-like behavior. IL-18, a member of the IL-1 superfamily, is primarily produced by activated macrophages, dendritic cells, and epithelial cells. It plays multifaceted roles in immune function, energy metabolism, and psychiatric disorders. In animal models, IL-18 mRNA expression is significantly elevated in the neocortex of rats subjected to social defeat, a model of stress and depressive behavior. Additionally, IL-18 mRNA and protein are expressed in several brain regions involved in mood regulation, including the pituitary gland, hippocampus, hypothalamus, and cerebral cortex. A meta-analysis encompassing 107 clinical studies with 5166 depressed patients revealed significantly higher IL-18 levels in depressed individuals compared to controls (g = 1.97; 95% CI: 1.00-2.95). A systematic review and meta-analysis of 45 studies further showed that circulating IL-18 concentrations were notably elevated in post-stroke depressed patients during the acute phase, compared to non-depressed stroke patients. Additionally, the prevalence of the C allele of IL18 rs187238 and the G allele of rs1946518 was significantly higher in individuals who experienced stressful life events. Furthermore, a Mendelian randomization study found a bidirectional causal relationship between genetically determined IL-18 levels and depression risk, underscoring its potential as a biomarker for depression. Given these findings, IL-18 plays a crucial role in the diagnostic prediction model for depression in this study, demonstrating its importance as a diagnostic biomarker.

Another key pro-inflammatory cytokine, IL-8, is secreted by various cell types, including macrophages and microglia, and triggers multiple intracellular signaling pathways by activating G-protein-coupled receptors, CXCR1 and CXCR2. IL-8 is produced early in the inflammatory response and can persist for days to weeks, making it specifically associated with chronic inflammatory processes that may lead to neuropsychological alterations in the brain. A systematic review of 56 clinical studies found that inflammatory markers, including IL-8, were strongly linked to prenatal depression. Additionally, a review on late-onset depression suggested that IL-8 levels could serve as a biomarker for predicting future depressive symptoms in older adults. However, some studies have not observed significant differences in IL-8 levels between MDD and HC. On the other hand, a longitudinal study of 732 older adults found that MDD was significantly associated with higher serum IL-8 levels at both baseline and two-year follow-up. Furthermore, a study involving first-episode, medication-naive depressed patients showed significantly elevated plasma IL-8 levels at baseline, with a marked decrease after 12 weeks of antidepressant treatment. These findings collectively support the involvement of IL-8 in depression development. In line with these studies, the results of the diagnostic prediction model in this study reaffirm IL-8's significant role as a diagnostic biomarker for MDD.

Another inflammation-associated protein identified in this study as a potential diagnostic aid for depression is MMP-8 (matrix metalloproteinase 8), also known as neutrophil collagenase. MMP-8 is primarily secreted by neutrophils and plays a critical role in mediating inflammation through the regulation of biologically active mediators such as interleukins and components of the complement system. In a recent study by Cathomas et al., published in Nature, it was reported that mice exposed to social stress showed significantly elevated levels of MMP-8 in their circulating immune cells. This increase led to alterations in the extracellular space and neuronal activity, which subsequently affected social behavior in the mice. These behavioral deficits resembled symptoms of depression, highlighting the potential of MMP-8 as both a diagnostic marker and therapeutic target for depression. Further support for MMP-8's role in depression was provided by Spengler et al., who also linked MMP-8 to depressive-like behaviors. Additionally, a study analyzing 21 genes shared by inflammatory bowel disease-associated secretory proteins and depression-related genes identified MMP-8 as one of four diagnostic-value genes, along with HGF, SPARC, and ADAM12. This study validated the accuracy of the model using ROC curves from an independent external dataset. While research on MMP-8 in depression is still limited, existing studies consistently underscore its significant diagnostic value for depression, aligning with the findings of this study.

passages.text: CD40, a tumor necrosis factor receptor superfamily member 5 (TNFRSF5), is a 45-50 kDa type I transmembrane protein that is widely expressed in B lymphocytes, antigen-presenting cells, and endothelial cells. Its ligand, CD40L (CD40 ligand), is a 39 kDa type II transmembrane protein primarily expressed in activated T cells, B cells, platelets, and natural killer cells. The CD40-CD40L receptor-ligand pair plays a crucial role in the adaptive immune response. Previous studies have observed elevated levels of soluble CD40 ligand (sCD40L) in patients with depression. Similar findings were reported by Neubauer et al.. A recent Mendelian randomization analysis exploring the genetic relationship between 731 immune cells and depression found a significant association between CD40 on CD14-CD16+ monocytes and depression risk (OR = 0.987, 95% CI = 0.981-0.993, P = 2.1 x 10-4). Furthermore, in a multicenter study with longitudinal follow-up, depressed patients treated with electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) showed a significant reduction in CD40 ligand levels 30 min after the first treatment. Additionally, activation of the brain-gut AMPK signaling pathway via CD40 may offer an important therapeutic strategy for depressed patients. The accumulated evidence from these studies further supports the potential clinical utility of CD40 as a marker for distinguishing depressed patients from non-depressed individuals.

passages.text: CASP-8 (Caspase-8) is a cysteine-type endopeptidase that plays a crucial role in apoptosis and inflammation signaling pathways. As a key protein in the exogenous apoptosis pathway, CASP-8 activates downstream effectors through binding to death receptors such as Fas and TNF receptors, thus initiating apoptosis. In addition to its role in apoptosis, CASP-8 is involved in the inflammatory response, where it regulates immune cell activation and cytokine release. A study involving 81 chronic pain patients demonstrated that CASP-8, along with other inflammatory proteins, was significantly associated with anxiety and depression. Furthermore, a Mendelian randomization analysis revealed a causal relationship between CASP-8 levels and the risk of depression. These findings, along with the results of the present study, highlight CASP-8 as a promising candidate biomarker for depression. In this study, CASP-8, along with other inflammation-related proteins, contributed to the development of a predictive model for depression diagnosis.

Insomnia is a prevalent sleep disorder characterized by difficulty falling asleep, maintaining sleep, or waking up too early and being unable to fall back asleep. These disturbances lead to poor sleep quality and daytime fatigue. Insomnia is not only a symptom of depression but also contributes to or exacerbates depressive symptoms, complicating treatment and often being the most common residual symptom in patients who are not fully in remission. Increasing evidence indicates that insomnia serves as an independent risk factor for both the first episode and recurrence of depression. In a large epidemiological study (n = 7954), individuals with persistent insomnia (insomnia present at baseline and at 1-year follow-up) were found to have a significantly higher likelihood of experiencing a new depressive episode at follow-up, compared to those whose insomnia resolved during the study (OR = 39.8, 95% CI = 19.8-80.0). A meta-analysis by Baglioni et al. found that insomnia predicted the risk of depression with an OR of 2.60 (95% CI: 1.98-3.42). Similarly, Saxbe et al. used structural equation modeling to explore the relationship between sleep quality and postpartum depression, revealing that poorer sleep quality significantly predicted more severe depressive symptoms at 6 and 12 months postpartum. Recent meta-analyses of 34 cohort studies with 172,077 participants further confirmed a strong link between insomnia and depression. Furthermore, machine learning analyses from the UK Biobank cohort (N = 64,353) indicate that subjective and objective sleep and circadian parameters serve as significant predictors of depression-related outcomes. Given the substantial evidence supporting insomnia as a predictor of depression, this study incorporates insomnia as an adjunctive diagnostic feature in the depression prediction model.

Cognitive impairment is a crucial feature of MDD, alongside affective symptoms. Cognitive deficits in depressed patients are often manifested as inattention, reduced verbal and nonverbal learning abilities, impaired short-term and working memory, and slower visual and auditory processing speeds, and are closely linked to the prognosis of MDD. Even after mood symptoms improve, many patients continue to struggle with cognitive deficits. A systematic review of first-episode depression and cognitive functioning found that cognitive deficits were already present in individuals experiencing their first depressive episode, and those with multiple episodes exhibited more severe cognitive impairment compared to those with a single episode. Additionally, a two-year follow-up study of individuals with recurrent depression revealed a consistent increase in self-reported cognitive difficulties correlated with higher levels of MDD and greater dysfunction throughout the follow-up period. These findings underline the significant role of cognitive functioning in the prediction and diagnosis of MDD.

EEG microstates, as an electrophysiological indicator, provide valuable insights for accurately diagnosing MDD. In this study, the diagnostic prediction model successfully identified the mean duration of microstate D as a key diagnostic feature. A resting-state EEG study on 93 depressed patients and 79 healthy controls found that both the duration and onset of microstate D were significantly reduced in the MDD compared to the HC, with Cohen's D values of 0.43 and 0.58, respectively. Furthermore, the proportion and duration of microstate D were negatively correlated with symptom severity (Spearman's rho of -0.34 and -0.46, respectively). Another study involving 101 depressed patients and 45 healthy controls reported that at baseline, depressed patients had shorter durations of microstate D compared to controls; however, after 8 weeks of treatment, both the duration and coverage of microstate D increased in the MDD. These findings highlight the potential of the mean duration of microstate D as an important neurophysiological marker to aid in the diagnosis of MDD. The integration of EEG-based cognitive biomarkers with machine learning for predicting depression also undoubtedly holds great promise.

This study has several limitations. First, it was a single-center observational study with a relatively small sample size, which limits the generalizability of the findings. Second, the follow-up period was short (4 weeks), which may not have fully captured the long-term trends of the indicators being studied. Third, there were limitations in the scientific management of clinical drug therapy, which may have influenced the study's results and affected the consistency of treatment across participants. Fourth, the validation analysis was conducted using follow-up observations from patients originally included in the training cohort; this internal dependency may have introduced model overfitting and consequently overestimated the apparent goodness of fit. These factors suggest that larger, multi-center studies with longer follow-up periods and more rigorous control of treatment protocols are needed to confirm and expand on these findings.
Conclusion

Individuals who exhibit insomnia, cognitive impairment (particularly in visuospatial/constructional), significant alterations in the mean duration of EEG microstate D, and dysregulated levels of inflammation-related proteins (such as IL-18, IL-8, MMP-8, CASP-8, and CD40) may show characteristics suggestive of depressive episodes. The multidimensional diagnostic prediction model developed in this study offers a valuable reference for the clinical realization of a more accurate and objective diagnosis of depression, integrating various biomarkers and neurophysiological indicators. This model may be valuable in improving the accuracy of depression diagnoses and enabling more personalized, effective interventions in clinical practice.

passages.text: Systemic Treatment for Hepatocellular Carcinoma Recurrence After Liver Transplantation
Simple Summary

Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. Liver transplantation (LT) represents the only curative treatment for both HCC and the underlying liver disease; however, post-transplant recurrence occurs in 8-20% of recipients and is associated with a poor prognosis. The management of recurrent HCC after LT is particularly challenging due to the need for lifelong immunosuppression, which may promote tumor progression and limit therapeutic options. In patients with advanced or multifocal recurrence, systemic therapy is the mainstay of treatment. Optimization of immunosuppressive regimens, particularly calcineurin inhibitor minimization and selective use of mTOR inhibitors, is critical.
Abstract

Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, and liver transplantation (LT) remains the only curative treatment addressing both tumor burden and underlying liver disease. Despite an adequate candidate selection, HCC recurrence after LT occurs in 8-20% of cases and is associated with a poor prognosis, particularly in patients who experience an early relapse. The management of HCC recurrence remains particularly challenging due to the lifelong immunosuppression required after LT, which may promote tumor progression and restrict therapeutic options. This review synthesizes the current evidence on systemic therapies for recurrent HCC after LT, focusing on tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), immunotherapy, and the current available immunosuppression strategies. Unfortunately, in this setting, robust prospective studies are lacking, and clinical decision-making remains based on retrospective data and expert consensus. Future research should prioritize the prospective evaluation of systemic regimens, integration of immunosuppression modulation, and careful exploration of immunotherapy or new target therapies in this special population.
1. Introduction

Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a major contributor to cancer-related morbidity and mortality worldwide, being the sixth most common diagnosis of cancer and the third most common cause of death in 2020.

Liver transplantation (LT) remains the only therapeutic approach with curative potential for both HCC and the underlying liver disease. It should be considered not only in patients with early-stage HCC but also in appropriately selected patients with multifocal or locally advanced tumors after a successful downstaging. The implementation of stringent selection criteria, such as the Milan criteria, and subsequent expanded criteria, has substantially improved post-transplant survival rates. However, despite the careful selection of candidates, HCC recurrence post-LT remains a challenge, as it occurs in approximately 8-20% of recipients and is associated with limited treatment options and a poor prognosis, with a median survival of 7 to 16 months. Most recurrences are diagnosed during the first 2-3 years. Early recurrence (<12 months) is a strong predictor of poor outcomes, while late recurrence is associated with better survival and is more amenable to curative intent treatment with superior survival outcomes. HCC recurrence has been associated with several oncological risk factors, such as tumor burden at LT, histological aggressiveness, vascular invasion and alpha-fetoprotein levels, as well as several non-oncological risk factors, including immunosuppressive drug exposure or CMV reactivation after LT. The management of HCC recurrence is extremely challenging as the post-transplant setting is characterized by the need to maintain a lifelong immunosuppression to prevent graft rejection. However, immunosuppressive drugs can influence tumor biology, impact on drug-drug interactions, and limit the efficacy and safety of potential treatment options, from surgery to systemic agents. Immunosuppression withdrawal has been theorized to lower the risk of oncologic relapse, constituting a potentially significant benefit in the management of post-transplant recurrence.

A tailored approach is recommended, where therapeutic decisions are made according to disease and patient-specific variables, including the timing and pattern of recurrence, patient outcomes, graft function, and biological markers. A multidisciplinary team (MDT) including transplant hepatologists, surgeons, oncologists, and radiologists is important to maintain the complex balance between oncological efficacy and the preservation of the liver allograft. Patients with limited, oligometastatic recurrence, a good performance status (ECOG 0-1), and preserved liver graft function (Child-Pugh A, ALBI grade 1) are suitable candidates for treatment, primarily surgical resection. In patients with recurrent HCC following liver transplantation, those having well-differentiated tumors and an absence of microvascular involvement have the most favorable outcomes following surgical resection, with one-year survival rates greater than 70%. Patients unsuitable for surgery may be considered for locoregional therapies, although these approaches are less effective in the presence of poorly differentiated tumors and microvascular involvement. However, patients with advanced, multifocal or multi-metastatic disease, with a poorer performance status (ECOG >= 2), or impaired graft function (Child-Pugh B and/or clinically significant portal hypertension) should be candidates for systemic treatments or palliative care (Figure 1).

The advent of tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), such as Sorafenib (SOF) and Lenvatinib (LEN), provided the first effective systemic options for advanced HCC. Consequently, TKIs have also been applied in the post-transplant setting, mostly at a personalized dose due to the comorbidities and concomitant medications of LT patients. More recently, the scenario of advanced HCC treatment has been completely changed by the advent of immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-based regimens, like Atezolizumab/Bevacizumab (A/B) or Durvalumab/Tremelimumab (DT). ICI-based treatments are superior to TKIs in terms of overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS). Consequently, these treatments have become the first-line therapy in non-transplant populations with unresectable or advanced HCC. However, their application in transplant recipients is challenging due to the risk of inducing allograft rejection and consequently data on the use of ICIs in transplanted patients are scarce. Historically, the LT population has been excluded from clinical trials evaluating novel cancer therapies, leading to a paucity of high-level evidence to guide clinical decision-making.

This literature review aims to comprehensively evaluate the current evidence for systemic treatment strategies for HCC recurrence after LT. We will critically examine the efficacy and safety of TKIs, discuss the challenges and limited role of immunotherapy, the role of immunosuppression in the management of patients with HCC recurrence and explore emerging therapeutic considerations and future directions for optimizing outcomes in this special population. A comprehensive understanding of systemic therapeutic strategies in the context of sustained chronic immunosuppression is pivotal for optimizing clinical outcomes in patients with HCC recurrence after LT.
Hepatocellular carcinoma recurrence after liver transplantation: treatment possibilities according to disease recurrence.
2. Methods

A literature review was conducted by searching the PubMed database using the keywords "hepatocellular carcinoma", "HCC recurrence", "liver transplantation" and "systemic therapy". Studies published in English that addressed recurrence of HCC after liver transplantation were included. Reference lists of eligible articles were also screened to identify additional relevant studies. Relevant information was extracted from selected studies, including study design, patient characteristics, immunosuppressive regimens, and the main oncological outcomes following liver transplantation.
3. TKI Treatment

Tyrosine kinase inhibitors have been the gold-standard for advanced HCC since 2007. TKIs act by binding to the active site of tyrosine kinases, preventing the phosphorylation of target proteins and subsequently downgrading signal transduction. In HCC, the blockade of key tyrosine kinase pathways:particularly those involving vascular endothelial growth factor receptors (VEGFRs), epidermal growth factor receptors (EGFR/ERBB), and platelet-derived growth factor receptors (PDGFRs):can effectively suppress tumor growth and angiogenesis. The primary molecular targets of TKIs in HCC include VEGFRs, PDGFRs, and other receptor tyrosine kinases involved in tumor vascularization and proliferation. TKIs exert their effects through either reversible or irreversible binding to various domains of receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), thereby inhibiting receptor activation. This inhibition disrupts downstream signaling cascades, including the MAPK, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, and JAK/STAT pathways, resulting in reduced tumor cell growth, proliferation, and metastasis. An overview of the major tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) investigated in HCC, along with their efficacy in general and immunosuppressed patients, is summarized in Table 1.

Despite immunotherapy having largely supplanted TKIs in the treatment of HCC, TKIs remain particularly relevant for transplant recipients due to the risk of liver graft rejection associated with immunotherapy. This aspect will be discussed in more detail below. Prospective ongoing studies about the use of TKI agents for the treatment of HCC recurrence are reported in Table 2.
3.1. Sorafenib

Systemic treatments for the recurrence of HCC after LT are based on therapies targeting multiple tyrosine kinases. Among them, SOF is a multi-kinase inhibitor that interferes with tumor cell proliferation and angiogenesis by blocking RAF kinases, vascular endothelial growth factor receptors (VEGFRs), and platelet-derived growth factor receptors (PDGFRs). SOF was the first agent to demonstrate a survival benefit in patients with advanced or unresectable HCC. In two Phase III randomized trials, SOF improved median OS by approximately three months compared to placebo (OS 10.7 vs. 7.9 months, p < 0.001 in the SHARP trial vs. OS 6.5 vs. 4.2 months, p = 0.014 in the Asia-Pacific trial). However, LT recipients were excluded from these pivotal registration trials; therefore, evidence in this population is largely derived from retrospective observational studies. Since 2009, several case series have assessed the safety and efficacy of SOF in LT recipients with HCC recurrence, both as monotherapy and in combination with mTOR inhibitors (mTOR-Is), given their dual immunosuppressive and antitumor properties. Sposito et al. have demonstrated that SOF improves the OS of patients with HCC recurrence after LT who were not suitable for surgery or radiotherapy (10.6 vs. 2.2 months) compared to best supportive care (BSC). Similar findings were also reported in an Asian population cohort. Kang et al. have confirmed that SOF significantly improved median post-transplant survival in patients with HCC recurrence (14.2 vs. 6.8 months) compared to BSC, with an acceptable toxicity profile. A similar study reported that patients treated with SOF for HCC recurrence achieved a disease control rate of 73.4%, with a one-year OS rate of 60%. The efficacy of SOF has been further corroborated by a large multicenter retrospective study involving 81 post-transplant patients, which reported a median OS of approximately 19 months following initiation of TKI therapy. The improved prognosis reported in the most recent publications has been attributed to a superior performance status, the application of multimodal or sequential treatment strategies and a better management of TKI-related adverse events. High-risk pathological features such as poor differentiation and vascular invasion predict recurrence risk after LT. However, no studies have demonstrated that specific histological subtypes significantly influence Sorafenib efficacy in the post-LT recurrence context. Vascular invasion is a well-established prognostic risk factor of HCC recurrence after LT. However, evidence supporting its role as a predictive factor for response to Sorafenib in the setting of post-transplant recurrence remains limited. In the general population, macrovascular invasion is associated with poorer survival and may correlate with reduced Sorafenib efficacy, reflecting a more aggressive tumor biology. However, Sposito et al. demonstrated that vascular invasion was not independently associated with survival after recurrence, and the benefit of Sorafenib was maintained regardless of vascular invasion.

passages.text: mTOR-Is, commonly used as immunosuppressive agents, target complementary signaling pathways implicated in HCC progression, providing synergistic antitumor and immunosuppressive effects. Consequently, several studies have investigated combination therapies with mTOR-Is and TKIs to enhance treatment efficacy. A retrospective study by Gomez-Martin et al. reported that the combination of SOF and mTOR-Is appears to be more effective than SOF alone in terms of OS (21.3 vs. 11.8 months). The authors reported minor and manageable adverse events (grade 1-2), although two serious bleeding complications were reported, highlighting the need for a careful risk assessment of bleeding risk in this population. The safety of early SOF administration in LT recipients has been evaluated in an Italian cohort including 50 patients. SOF-related adverse events (AEs) occurred in all treated patients, 56% of them being grade 3-4. There was no significant difference in SOF-related AEs between patients taking mTOR-Is or other immunosuppressive regimens, except for hand-foot syndrome. In this cohort, the use of mTOR-Is and SOF was associated with an increase in OS in univariate analysis but not in multivariate analysis. Thus, SOF represents the most extensively studied systemic therapy for HCC recurrence after LT, demonstrating a survival benefit over BSC in retrospective studies, both as monotherapy and in combination with mTOR-Is. However, considering several adverse effects related to SOF treatment, a careful individualized assessment is required.
3.2. Regorafenib

Regorafenib (REG) is an oral multi-kinase inhibitor used in the treatment of various types of oncological diseases, including colorectal cancer, gastrointestinal stromal tumors and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). REG is an oral diphenyl urea multi-kinase inhibitor that targets angiogenic (VEGFR1-3, TIE2), stromal (PDGFR-beta, FGFR), and oncogenic receptor tyrosine kinases (KIT, RET, and RAF). In the setting of HCC, REG proved to be particularly effective in increasing OS in patients with progressive disease after SOF with a good toxicity profile. Similar efficacy has been demonstrated in LT recipients with HCC recurrence after LT. In a multicenter observational retrospective study, Iavarone et al. reported no life-threatening or unexpected adverse events attributable to REG administration in an LT population. In this study, the majority of AEs were classified as mild or moderate (Grade 1 or 2 according to CTCAE grading), and notably, no cases of hepatic graft rejection were recorded. REG was associated with a median OS of approximately 12.9 months. When considering sequential therapy with SOF followed by REG, the median OS extended to 38.4 months. These results have been further confirmed in 2021 in a larger multicenter study. Patients receiving REG as a second-line treatment after SOF exhibited a median OS of approximately 28.8 months, compared to a median OS of 15.3 months in patients who did not receive REG. REG was generally well tolerated in LT recipients, with adverse events being manageable. The combination of mTOR-Is with REG was not associated with any significant impact on OS in LT patients with HCC recurrence. In a more recent multicenter analysis, Ozbay et al. reported that the median OS for patients treated sequentially with SOF followed by REG was 35.9 months, demonstrating an improvement in OS compared to the previous studies. In conclusion, REG appears to positively impact OS with an acceptable safety profile and can be considered a valid second-line treatment option for patients with HCC recurrence after LT who have progressed on SOF.
