passages.text: 3.3. STG Promotes Osteogenic Differentiation of MC3T3-E1 Cells

To observe the effects of STG on osteogenic differentiation, we treated MC3T3-E1 cells with different concentrations of STG under the condition of osteogenic induction. Western blot analysis revealed that, compared with the control group, 2.5-10 muM STG significantly increased the protein expression level of the osteogenic marker OCN, while the osteogenic marker RUNX2 showed a more pronounced expression at 5-10 muM (Figure 5A,B). Furthermore, ALP activity assessed on day 14 and matrix mineralization evaluated via ARS staining on day 21 were both markedly enhanced in the STG-treated groups compared to the control group (Figure 5C). These results indicate that STG can dose-dependently promote the osteogenic differentiation of MC3T3-E1 cells. However, its specific molecular targets and mechanisms of action remain unclear and require further investigation.
3.4. Network Pharmacology Analysis of STG and OP
3.4.1. Identification of STG and OP-Related Targets

Potential protein targets of STG were retrieved by integrating data from the COREMINE, TCMSP, and Swiss Target Prediction databases. After removing duplicate items, 686 different STG candidate targets were identified. At the same time, genes related to OP were obtained from the specialized databases of GeneCards and OMIM. After this, 2055 non-repetitive targets were identified. The common targets were obtained by intersecting the 686 STG targets with the 2055 OP-related targets. Visualization in a Venn diagram revealed 278 overlapping targets, which were identified as possible key targets for STG in OP treatment (Figure 6A).
3.4.2. PPI Network

The 278 cross-target nodes in the figure were input into the STRING database (version 11.0), with the minimum interaction score threshold set to >0.7. Cytoscape was used to draw a network diagram of protein interactions, as shown in Figure 6B. There are 269 nodes and 3132 connecting lines in this network.
3.4.3. GO and KEGG Pathway Enrichment Analysis

To further investigate the biological role of STG in the treatment of OP, we conducted Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses of the target genes using the Weishengxin platform. As illustrated in Figure 6D, the GO biological process (GO-BP) analysis suggests that STG may be associated with several biological processes, including the positive regulation of kinase activity, the positive regulation of the MAPK cascade, the enzyme-linked receptor protein signaling pathway, the positive regulation of protein phosphorylation, the positive regulation of cell migration, and the response to oxidative stress. The GO cellular component (GO-CC) analysis indicates that the cellular components involved in STG's action against OP are primarily located in membrane structures, vesicles, and the endoplasmic reticulum. The GO molecular function (GO-MF) analysis suggests that STG may be related to molecular functions such as protein kinase activity, growth factor binding, and cytokine receptor binding. Consequently, the genes regulated by STG are likely to play a significant role in the secretion of relevant cytokines and the regulation of protein activity. Figure 6C presents the pathways associated with STG in the treatment of OP, as identified through the KEGG enrichment analysis. These pathways include the PI3K-Akt, HIF-1A, MAPK, JAK-STAT, NF-kappaB, ErbB, and Wnt signaling pathways.
3.4.4. Screening of Key Targets

Cluster analysis was performed using the MCODE plugin in Cytoscape 3.9.0 software, with the top three subnetworks selected (Figure 7A), yielding a total of 91 key targets. Details are provided in Table 1. The betweenness centrality, closeness centrality, and degree centrality of each network node were analyzed using the topological features of Cytoscape 3.9.0. The results of this topological analysis revealed that the target proteins with higher degree values included EGF, TP53, AKT1, and STAT3. Subsequently, the CytoHubba plugin was employed to screen the top 15 network nodes using the MCC method, which were classified as the hub genes associated with STG in the treatment of OP. These hub genes included STAT3, JUN, TP53, ESR1, EGF, TNF, MYC, IL2, and JAK2 (Figure 7B).
3.5. STG Promotes Osteogenic Differentiation via the JAK2/STAT3 Signaling Pathway

To investigate the impact of STG on the JAK2/STAT3 signaling pathway in MC3T3-E1 cells, we employed AutoDock Vina docking software to analyze the molecular interactions between STG and components of the JAK2/STAT3 pathway. Our docking analysis revealed binding energies of -9.5 kcal/mol for the STG-JAK2 interaction and -7.4 kcal/mol for the STG-STAT3 interaction (Figure 8A). Additionally, we examined the expression of relevant genes using Western blot analysis (Figure 8B,C). The results indicated that, compared to the STG (-) AG490 (-) group, the protein levels of p-JAK2 and p-STAT3 were significantly elevated in the STG (+) AG490 (-) group. These findings suggest that a STG concentration of 10 mumol/L effectively activates the JAK2/STAT3 signaling pathway. AG490 is an inhibitor of the JAK2/STAT3 signaling pathway, and it was utilized to further investigate the involvement of this pathway in the osteogenic differentiation process induced by STG. The results indicated that, compared to the STG (-) AG490 (-) group, the protein expressions of p-JAK2 and p-STAT3 in the STG (-) AG490 (+) group were significantly reduced. Furthermore, when comparing the STG (+) AG490 (-) group with the STG (+) AG490 (+) group, it was found that the reduction in the protein expression of p-JAK2 and p-STAT3 induced by STG was significantly enhanced after treatment with 50 mumol/L AG490. These findings indicate that AG490 effectively inhibits the JAK2/STAT3 signaling pathway activated by STG.

Osteogenic assay results demonstrated that, compared with the STG (-) AG490 (-) group, the protein levels of OCN and RUNX2 were significantly elevated in the STG (+) AG490 (-) group, while the protein expression of OCN and RUNX2 was significantly reduced in the STG (-) AG490 (+) group. Compared with the STG (+) AG490 (-) group, the STG (+) AG490 (+) group also exhibited significantly reduced STG-induced protein expression of OCN and RUNX2 after treatment with 50 mumol/L AG490 (Figure 9A,B). The ALP and ARS staining results demonstrated that, compared with the STG (-) AG490 (-) group, the staining areas of ALP and ARS were significantly increased in the STG (+) AG490 (-) group, while they were significantly decreased in the STG (-) AG490 (+) group. Similarly, the staining areas were significantly decreased in the STG (+) AG490 (+) group compared with the STG (+) AG490 (-) group (Figure 9C). Thus, the JAK2/STAT3 signaling pathway may play a role in the osteogenic differentiation of MC3T3-E1 cells promoted by STG.
4. Discussion

This study systematically evaluated the therapeutic potential of STG for OP using an ovariectomized rat model. Micro-CT analysis revealed that STG intervention significantly reversed estrogen deficiency-induced bone microstructural deterioration, manifested as increased BMD, BV/TV, and Tb.N, alongside decreased Tb.Sp. Notably, STG not only enhanced bone mass but also improved trabecular connectivity and spatial architecture:critical for maintaining bone biomechanical strength and resilience. At the model validation level, it was observed that serum E2 levels in the OVX group were significantly lower than those in the sham group, but E2 in the OVX group was not completely eliminated. This finding confirms that the sources of estrogen in the body are not limited to the ovaries; peripheral tissues such as the adrenal cortex, skin, adipose tissue, and hypothalamus also possess the ability to synthesize estrogen or convert androgens into E2 via the aromatase pathway. Simultaneously, this indicates that the OVX model simulates a state of "relative estrogen deficiency" rather than absolute deficiency. Despite these circumstances, the significant reduction in E2 levels in the OVX group remains sufficient to establish it as a classic animal model for studying OP. STG demonstrated significant bone-protective effects even under partial estrogen deficiency, suggesting that it may act through estrogen-independent mechanisms or as a partial substitute pathway for estrogen signaling. H&E staining analysis further confirmed that STG effectively promoted trabecular bone mineralization, indicating that this compound may restore bone microstructural balance by enhancing bone formation rather than solely inhibiting bone resorption. IHC and IF detection revealed that STG restored RUNX2 and OCN expression levels in the bone marrow cavity of OVX rats. This finding aligns with the known mechanism of action of phytoestrogens: previous studies have indicated that various phytoestrogenic compounds (e.g., genistein and daidzein aglycone) promote osteoblastic differentiation by upregulating key transcription factors such as RUNX2. Furthermore, in vitro experiments demonstrated that STG significantly increased RUNX2 and OCN expression in MC3T3-E1 cells, thereby promoting osteoblast differentiation and mineralization processes.

To systematically elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying STG's anti-osteoporosis effects, this study employed network pharmacology methods to predict its potential targets and signaling pathways. An analysis suggested that STG may exert its OP therapeutic effects by activating multiple key targets, including STAT3, JUN, TP53, ESR1, EGF, TNF, MYC, IL2, and JAK2. GO enrichment analysis further revealed that STG participates in multiple biological processes, including the positive regulation of kinase activity, positive regulation of MAPK cascade, enzyme-linked receptor protein signaling pathway, positive regulation of protein phosphorylation, positive regulation of cell migration, and response to oxidative stress. KEGG pathway analysis indicated that STG may exert therapeutic effects by regulating signaling pathways closely associated with bone metabolism, including PI3K-Akt, HIF-1alpha, MAPK, JAK-STAT, NF-kappaB, ErbB, and Wnt. These predictive findings collectively outline STG's "multi-target, multi-pathway" action profile, consistent with its chemical structure as a natural plant sterol. Its multiple unsaturated double bonds and specific functional groups confer broad protein-binding capabilities. As a predictive tool, network pharmacology results require experimental validation. Therefore, this study further validated the predictions through molecular docking and in vitro cell experiments, focusing on the JAK2/STAT3 pathway. The results showed that STG exhibits stable binding conformations with both JAK2 and STAT3 proteins, with binding energies of -9.5 kcal/mol and -7.4 kcal/mol, respectively, suggesting its potential as a direct modulator of this signaling pathway. The regulatory role of the JAK2/STAT3 signaling pathway in bone metabolism exhibits cell-type specificity. Within the osteoblast lineage, activation of this pathway is typically associated with cell proliferation and early differentiation. This study observed that STG significantly upregulates the phosphorylation levels of JAK2 and STAT3 in MC3T3-E1 cells, accompanied by increased expression of RUNX2 and OCN. This relationship suggests the existence of a regulatory axis: "STG   JAK2/STAT3 phosphorylation   RUNX2 transcriptional activation   OCN expression   mineralization maturation". This inference is supported by AG490 inhibition experiments: JAK2-specific inhibition not only blocked STAT3 phosphorylation but also significantly suppressed expression of downstream osteogenic marker genes, confirming the pathway's necessity for STG effects. This finding mechanistically aligns with that of recent studies by Wang et al. using the JAK2/STAT3 pathway inhibitor AG490 and STAT3-silencing experiments, confirming that activation of this pathway is a prerequisite for osteogenic effects. However, the role of the JAK2/STAT3 signaling pathway in osteocytes is context-dependent. Notably, Xiong et al. demonstrated that SDF-1/CXCR4 promotes osteogenic differentiation in BMSCs by activating JAK2/STAT3; conversely, recent studies indicate that JAK2/STAT3 activation inhibits osteogenic transdifferentiation in vascular smooth muscle cells. This discrepancy may stem from cell-type-specific combinations of transcription factors or cross-talk with other signaling pathways. In this study, the findings regarding the pro-differentiating effect of STG on MC3T3-E1 pre-osteoblasts align with those of Xiong et al., though the specific molecular mechanism may differ: STG may initiate the signaling cascade by directly binding to the JAK2 kinase domain rather than through indirect activation mediated by G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs). Furthermore, the regulatory relationship between JAK2/STAT3 and RUNX2 warrants further investigation. Although a positive correlation in their expression was observed in this study, STAT3, as a transcription factor, may regulate RUNX2 either directly (by binding to the RUNX2 promoter region) or indirectly (by modulating other transcription factors such as Osterix) (Figure 10).

This study has several limitations. First, although the AG490 inhibition assay confirmed the necessity of the JAK2/STAT3 pathway, it does not rule out the possibility that STG may simultaneously act on other parallel pathways (such as Wnt/beta-catenin or PI3K/Akt). Although 50 muM is the classical concentration of AG490 that effectively inhibits JAK2/STAT3 phosphorylation in various cell lines, its interaction with other kinases cannot be entirely ruled out. Moreover, prolonged high-concentration treatment may also induce nonspecific cellular stress responses. Therefore, future studies will employ more selective JAK2 inhibitors (e.g., Fedratinib) or gene knockout techniques to further validate these findings and explore precision therapeutic strategies targeting this pathway. Second, molecular docking predictions indicate that STG possesses binding affinity for both JAK2 and STAT3, yet precise binding affinity and dissociation constants (Kd) remain undetermined via biophysical methods such as surface plasmon resonance (SPR) or isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC). Finally, characteristics including STG's in vivo bioavailability and metabolic stability will directly influence its potential for clinical translation. Future research should establish pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic (PK-PD) models to optimize dosing regimens.

In summary, this study integrated network pharmacology, molecular docking, and in vitro/in vivo experiments to reveal the molecular mechanism by which STG promotes osteogenic differentiation through activation of the JAK2/STAT3 signaling pathway. This discovery not only expands our understanding of plant sterols' regulatory role in bone metabolism but also provides experimental evidence for developing novel natural product-based strategies against OP. However, translating this mechanism discovery into clinical application requires overcoming multiple challenges, including pharmacodynamic optimization, safety assessment, and formulation development.
5. Conclusions

Based on the findings of this study, we conclude the following: The OVX-induced OP model is reliable, and the promotion of bone formation and osteoblast differentiation by STG in OP is confirmed, which provides a foundation for further research. Through multidimensional experimental evidence, including network pharmacology prediction, molecular docking simulations, and in vitro functional validation, we demonstrate that STG enhances osteoblast differentiation and mineralization maturation by activating the "JAK2/STAT3   RUNX2   OCN" regulatory axis. In summary, STG holds potential as a promising osteogenic promoter and therapeutic candidate for OP.

passages.text: Acute Inflammation Drives Corneal Pathological Regeneration
Purpose
This study aimed to characterize transcriptional and epigenetic remodeling in the cornea induced by acute inflammation.
Methods

Limbal-corneal tissues were collected on days 5 and 10 after intrastromal administration of lipopolysaccharide or PBS. ScRNA-seq and scATAC-seq were used to delineate the transcriptomic and epigenomic atlas of the inflamed cornea, following the Seurat and Signac pipelines. Immunofluorescence was performed to assess changes in corneal epithelial markers and immune cell infiltration.
Results

We identified 16 cell clusters, including ten epithelial cell subpopulations, keratocytes, fibroblasts, corneal endothelial cells, blood vessel cells, lymphatic vessel cells, and immune cells. Lipopolysaccharide induced the infiltration of five major immune cell types: neutrophils, MHC-II- macrophages, MHC-II+ macrophages, T cells, and natural killer cells. We characterized gene expression and chromatin accessibility dynamics across all cell types during the inflammatory response, revealing cell-type-specific gene regulatory elements and cis-regulatory chromatin interactions. Regulon activity and motif accessibility analyses identified critical transcription factors that drive distinct inflammatory response programs. Inflammation was found to inhibit limbal stem/progenitor cell differentiation. CellChat analysis revealed a set of secreted intercellular crosstalk signals among all cell types.
Conclusions

Our work provides a comprehensive, time-resolved single-cell transcriptomic and epigenomic atlas of the inflamed cornea, defining cellular functional heterogeneity, cis-regulatory networks, and intercellular communication during corneal pathological regeneration. These findings offer valuable insights into corneal pathology.

The cornea, located at the outermost part of the eyeball, is a transparent avascular structure composed of epithelium, stroma, and endothelium. The cornea is widely recognized as an immune-privileged tissue, endowed with constitutive expression of immunomodulatory molecules that protect optical clarity. Paradoxically, on mechanical, chemical or microbial injury, this privilege is rapidly revoked and diverse immune cell types infiltrate the cornea, provoking a vigorous inflammatory response that are tightly coupled to epithelial repair. However, the dynamics of the immune microenvironment induced by acute inflammation and how they contribute to corneal injury remain largely unknown.

The corneal epithelium, a self-renewing stratified squamous barrier essential for vision, is continuously replenished by limbal stem cells (LSCs) residing in the basal layer of the limbus. These LSCs orchestrate tissue homeostasis through asymmetric division, generating transient amplifying cells (TACs) that migrate centripetally to differentiate into mature corneal epithelial cells (CECs). Although the limbus contains blood vessels and a limited population of immune cells, LSCs are also in an immunosuppressive niche. However, LSCs exhibit exceptional sensitivity to inflammatory mediators. Pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., TNF-alpha, IL-1beta) released during injury or infection directly impair LSC homeostasis. Persistent inflammation disrupts the delicate balance between self-renewal and differentiation of LSCs, leading to stem cell exhaustion, delayed epithelial wound closure and ultimately, vision loss. Therefore the cornea offers a unique model to elucidate how immune activation instructs epithelial regeneration or, when dysregulated, precipitates stem cell exhaustion and tissue pathology.

Here, we generated a comprehensive transcriptomic and epigenomic atlas of the inflammatory response by integrating high-quality single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin sequencing (scATAC-seq) data from limbal-corneal tissues collected 5 and 10 days after intrastromal lipopolysaccharide (LPS) administration. The single-cell multi-omics atlas of inflamed limbal-corneal compartments reveals coordinated transcriptomic and epigenomic remodeling across epithelial and immune populations, with cell-type-specific cis-regulatory elements linked to functional states. Interestingly, we defined two temporally dynamic macrophage (MP) states (MHC-II+ and MHC-II-) with distinct transcription factor dependencies. The transcriptional and epigenetic landscapes of MHC-II- MPs were shaped by MAFB, MAF, and MITF, whereas those of MHC-II+ MPs were defined by BHLHE40, BCL11A, and NR4A2. MHC-II- MPs possessed both pro- and anti-inflammatory properties simultaneously. We also revealed the critical intercellular signaling communication networks among all cell types. Collectively, our work reveals detailed functional characteristics and molecular dynamics of diverse limbal-corneal epithelial and infiltrating immune cell populations under acute inflammation and provides new insights into corneal pathological regeneration.
Material and Methods
Human and Animal Ethics
All animal experiments were approved by the Animal Ethics Committee of the Zhongshan Ophthalmic Centre.
Animal Experiments

Female C57BL/6 mice (six to eight weeks old) were used in this study. For establishemnt of the LPS-induced corneal inflammation model, the mice were anaesthetized intraperitoneally with pentobarbital sodium (50 mg/kg) and then intrastromally injected with LPS (1 microg/microL, MCE, HY-D1056). PBS injections served as the control group.
Immunofluorescence and TUNEL Staining

For immunofluorescence staining, cell samples were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 10 minutes at room temperature. Tissue samples were sequentially fixed, dehydrated, paraffin embedded, deparaffinized, and antigen repaired as previously described. The cells or tissue sections were permeabilized and blocked with PBS solution containing 3% BSA and 0.3% Triton X-100 for one hour, followed by incubation with primary antibodies at 4 C overnight. Next, the samples were incubated with secondary antibodies and Hoechst 333258 dye (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). All slides were imaged using a ZEISS LSM 800 confocal laser scanning microscope. The antibodies used for immunofluorescence are as follows: anti-KRT3 (no. ab68260, 1:200; Abcam, Cambridge, MA, USA), anti-KRT12 (no. ab124975, 1:200; Abcam), anti-ALDH3A1 (no. GTX30042, 1:200; GeneTex, Inc., Irvine, CA, USA), anti-CLU (no. 12289-1-AP, 1:200; Proteintech, Rosemont, IL, USA), and anti-PAX6 (no. AMAB91372, 1:200; Sigma-Aldrich Corp., St. Louis, MO, USA). TUNEL staining was performed according to the manufacturer's instructions (no. C1086; Beyotime Institute of Biotechnology, Jiangsu, China).
Single Cell Dissociation and Sequencing

For each sample, 10 limbal-corneal tissues were collected and pooled. For scRNA-seq, the collected tissues were cut into small pieces on ice and then enzymatically digested at 37 C for 45 to 60 minutes. After the removal of red blood cells, the remaining cells were filtered through a 30 microm strainer. Dead cells were subsequently depleted using the MACS Dead Cell Removal Kit (Miltenyi Biotec, Bergisch Gladbach, Germany). The cDNA sequencing libraries were constructed using the Chromium Next GEM Single Cell 3' Reagent Kits v3.1 (10x Genomics, Pleasanton, CA, USA) following the manufacturer's protocol. Four independent biological replicates were performed for the control and LPS D10 groups, and three for the LPS D5 group. For scATAC-seq, single-nucleus suspensions were obtained according to the 10x Genomics Nuclei Isolation protocol and then run on the 10x Chromium Single Cell ATAC platform to construct scATAC-seq libraries. The Illumina Novaseq platform (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA) was used for library sequencing. Two independent biological replicates were performed for each group.
ScRNA-Seq Data Analysis

Sequencing reads were aligned to mouse mm 10 genome with Cell Ranger software to generate feature-barcode count matrices. R package Seurat was used for downstream analysis.We excluded cells that contained more than 15% mitochondrial reads or fewer than 300 detected genes. After the high-variable genes of each sample were identified using SCTransform workflow, all datasets were integrated using the FindIntegrationAnchors and IntegrateData functions with default parameters. Dimensionality reduction and clustering were performed according to Seurat pipeline. A scDblFinder package was used to remove doublets. The coarse immune cell type was extracted and re-analyzed to obtain more refined clustering using the same approach described above.

Marker genes for each cell type were identified by using FindAllMarkers function (min.pct = 0.5, logfc.threshold = 0.5, test.use = "MAST"), retaining those with a P-value < 0.05. The Spearman correlation among all cell types was calculated based on the average expression levels of marker genes within each cell population. The Findmarkers function was used for the identification of differentially expressed genes in each cell type (min.pct = 0.5, test.use = "MAST", logfc.threshold = 0.5). Differential enrichment of Gene Ontology terms was assessed by GSVA using a Gaussian model. The R package clusterProfiler was applied to Gene Ontology enrichment. Augur and CellChat analysis was performed according to official tutorials with default parameters. PySCENIC (Python implementation) was used to reconstruct cell-type-specific transcription factor regulon networks from the scRNA-seq dataset, using the raw UMI count matrix exported from Seurat as input. The RcisTarget mouse mm10 motif database was used. Pseudotime trajetory was inferred by Slingshot pipeline.
ScATAC-Seq Data Analysis

ScATAC-seq data analysis were performed according to Signac pipeline. We calculated the number of unique fragments and the enrichment at the transcription start sites in each cell, which were used for quality control. The Signac method of term frequency-inverse document frequency was used for data normalization. Then top variable features were identified using the FindTopFeatures function. Following iterative LSI dimensionality reduction, datasets were intergrated by Harmony algorithm. Signac's FindNeighbors and FindClusters functions were used for clustering with resolution = 3. We extracted the immune cells for reclustering using the same pipeline described above. Peaks were called by MACS2 algorithm. Doublets were removed using scDblFinder R package. Signac's FindAllMarkers and FindMarkers functions with test.use = "LR" were, respectively, used to identify marker peaks and differential peaks for each cell type. Transcription factor motif activities were inferred using the R package chromVAR. We used the Footprint function to infer the selected transcription factor footprint in each cell type. The chromatin co-accessibility network was identified by cicero framework.
Results
Inflammation Reprograms the Corneal Transcriptome and Epigenome

To explore the immune-epithelial interaction pattern, we induced corneal acute inflammation through intrastromal injection of LPS (Supplementary Fig. S1A). We found that the CEC markers KRT12, CLU and ALDH3A1 were partially lost on day 5 and completely undetectable by day 10, but the expression of PAX6 (a LSC cell fate determinant) was not affected (Fig. 1A). Few apoptotic cells were observed after LPS treatment (Supplementary Fig. S1B). To comprehensively investigate how inflammatory conditions contribute to pathological regeneration of the corneal epithelium, single cells isolated from limbal-corneal tissues on the fifth and tenth days after LPS administration and control samples were processed for scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq using the 10x Genomics platform. High transcriptional start site enrichment scores and large unique fragment counts in most cells per sample highlighted high-quality scATAC-seq data (Supplementary Fig. S1C). We obtained 98,922 single-cell transcriptomes and 67,945 single-cell chromatin accessibility profiles following quality control and doublet removal (Fig. 1B). After batch correction, dimensionality reduction and clustering, both transcriptomic and epigenomic datasets yielded 16 distinct cell populations annotated with the expression and gene activity scores (a quantitative measure of gene accessibility) of the well-known marker genes (Figs. 1 B, 1C; Supplementary Fig. S1D).

Single-cell atlas of gene expression and chromatin accessibility in the inflamed limbal-corneal tissues. (A) Immunofluorescence staining for the indicated genes in mouse corneal tissues at one, three, five, and 10 days after intrastromal injection of LPS. (B) Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) plots showing matched scRNA-seq (left) and scATAC-seq (right) cell types in the limbal-corneal compartments at five and 10 days after LPS treatment. (C) Dot plot showing marker genes of each cell type in scRNA-seq data. (D) Spearman correlation of expression and chromatin accessibility among all cell types. (E) Representative marker peaks identified in each cell type. (F) Genomic distribution of peaks for all cell types. (G) Proportion of each cell type in scRNA-seq data. (H, I) Augur scores across all cell types at day 5 and day 10 after inflammatory stimulation based on scRNA-seq (H) and scATAC-seq (I) data, respectively.

All cell clusters corresponded to epithelial, mesenchymal, endothelial and immune lineages. The limbal-corneal epithelium is composed of basal, suprabasal and superficial layers. We identified canonical limbal-corneal epithelial cell types including LSCs (Gpha2, Bcam, Trp63 and Ccnd2), corneal basal cells (Itgb4, Bcam, Ccnd1, Col17a1 and Gja1), corneal superficial cells (Tjp3, Muc20), limbal suprabasal cells (Krt4, Krt13, Krt19, Dsp, Dsc2) and limbal superficial cells (Krt4, Krt13, Krt19, Tjp3, Muc20). Three corneal suprabasal subpopulations were identified. Corneal suprabasal-1 and corneal suprabasal-3 clusters expressed Cldn4, Cdkn1a, Dsg1a, Dsp and Dsc2. The corneal suprabasal-1 cluster exhibited higher expression levels of Dapl1 and Gyg, whereas the corneal suprabasal-2 cluster had higher expression of Fabp5. Notably, two Birc5- and Top2a-positive TAC subpopulations derived from LSCs were defined, with the TAC-1 cluster showing expression of basal cell markers. The overall gene expression and accessible peaks of TAC-1 cluster exhibited a higher correlation with basal layer cells, while TAC-2 cluster was more correlated with LSCs (Figs. 1C, 1D), suggesting that the TAC-1 population was more differentiated. The molecular signatures of the corneal endothelium were more similar to blood vessels, lymphatic vessels and fibroblasts. The corneal suprabasal-3 subpopulation was highly correlated with the corneal superficial layer, indicative of a more differentiated state. In contrast, the corneal suprabasal-1 cluster was less differentiated due to the more correlated with TACs (Fig. 1D). To nominate putative cis-regulatory elements, we used MACS2 to call peak for each scATAC-seq cell and then merged all significant peaks, resulting in the identification of marker peaks for each cell type (Fig. 1E). Cell types with developmental proximity shared analogous chromatin landscapes. The majority of accessibility peaks were localized within promoter regions in the LSC, TAC-2, and blood-vessel clusters (Fig. 1F). In other cell types, peaks were predominantly enriched in introns and intergenic regions, which were suggestive of putative active enhancers.

We then explored the major changes induced by inflammation. Although few immune cells were observed in the control group, LPS administration resulted in substantial immune cell infiltration (Figs. 1B, 1G; Supplementary Fig. S1E). On the fifth day after the injury, the proportion of immune cells reached approximately 50%, which subsequently declined to around 8% by the tenth day. To investigate the dynamic response of limbal-corneal tissue to inflammatory stimuli, we applied Augur, a robust machine-learning framework prioritizing cell types most responsive to biological perturbations, to our scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq datasets. We found that gene expression in the corneal suprabasal-2 and immune-cell clusters exhibited pronounced alterations on the fifth day of the inflammation process, whereas these changes diminished by the tenth day (Fig. 1H). This pattern was consistent with their cellular proportions. Thus, inflammation was reduced significantly by the tenth day. However, the chromatin accessibility patterns of immune cells remained stable across the two time points (Fig. 1I). Most cell populations showed greater changes in transcriptome and epigenome at day 10 than at day 5 (Figs. 1H, 1I), suggesting a delayed injury of limbal-corneal tissues. Gene expression in the LSC, corneal suprabasal-1, and superficial populations was most sensitive to inflammatory stimuli (Fig. 1H).
Dynamic Changes of Immune Microenvironment Under Inflammatory Stimulation

To better resolve the heterogeneity of the infiltrating immune system, we reclustered the coarse immune cell population, generating five major immune cell classes (neutrophils, MHC-II+ MPs, MHC-II- MPs, T cells and NK cells) annotated with the well-known markers in both scRNA and scATAC datasets (Figs. 2A-C). They were few in the control group and increased substantially after LPS administration. Neutrophils (marked by Csf3r, S100a8, and S100a9) were most abundant on day 5 after injury but declined sharply by day 10 (Figs. 2A, 2B, 2D; Supplementary Fig. S2A), suggesting a key early role in the inflammation response. In contrast, the two MP subpopulations, along with T and NK cells, maintained expansion at both time points, indicating their sustained or ongoing involvement throughout the immune response process. Each cell type showed a cohort of specific marker genes and peaks (Fig. 2E; Supplementary Fig. S2B). The genome-wide distribution pattern of accessibility peaks was similar in all immune cell types, with a high proportion at promoters (Fig. 2F).

Transcriptional and epigenetic landscape of corneal immune microenvironment under inflammatory stimulation. (A, B) UMAP plots showing re-clustered immune cell types in scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq data. (C) Dot plot showing expression and gene activity of representative marker genes in all immune cell populations. (D) Milo analysis for differential abundance of the indicated immune cell types between samples treated with the indicated conditions in scRNA-seq data. FC, fold change; FDR, false discovery rate. (E) Representative marker peaks identified by MACS2 in each immune cell type. (F) Genomic distribution of peaks identified in all immune cell types. (G) Augur scores across all immune cell populations at day 5 and day 10 after inflammatory stimulation, based on scRNA-seq data. (H) Gene ontology enrichment analysis for marker peaks of MHC-II- MPs, MHC-II+ MPs and neutrophils. (I) Genomic tracks showing chromatin accessibility around the indicated gene loci across all immune cell types. Peaks called in the scATAC data and peak-to-gene links identified by Cicero framework are indicated below the tracks. Relative scRNA-seq expression of the corresponding genes is shown in the violin plots. (J) The differentially expressed genes of each immune cell type between day 5 and day 10 after LPS treatment.

MPs represent the predominant population of resident immune cells in the healthy cornea. Two MP subpopulations (MHC-II+ and MHC-II-) were observed. MHC-II+ MPs were Cd74 positive, and MHC-II- MPs were Cd93, Cd84 and Stab1 positive (Fig. 2C; Supplementary Fig. S2C). Augur analysis showed that MHC-II- MPs underwent the most pronounced changes in gene expression in response to external stimuli (Fig. 2G). MHC-II- MPs had the largest number of marker genes (Supplementary Fig. S2B), highlighting their functional diversity. Thus we speculated that MHC-II- MPs may be important for wound healing. We then performed Gene Ontology analysis for marker peaks of each immune cell type. We observed that MHC-II- MPs displayed pro-inflammatory and proliferative properties, as evidenced by the enrichment of biological processes related to positive regulation of cell cycle, p38 MAPK cascade, ERK1/ERK2 cascade, lymphocyte differentiation, NF-kappaB signaling and the production of chemokine, interferon-gamma, IL-6 and TNF (Fig. 2H). They were also implicated in phagocytosis, endocytosis, autophagy, lipid metabolism, peptide hormone secretion, Wnt and Notch signaling pathways and response to TGF-beta, steroid, cGAMP and insulin. Only MHC-II+ MPs showed a greater change in gene expression on day 10 compared to day 5 following the injury (Fig. 2G). MHC-II+ MPs expressed genes related to calcium ion transport, leukocyte cell-cell adhesion, response to TGF-beta, TGF-beta receptor, Wnt and proteinkinase B signaling, phagocytosis, and interferon-gamma production (Fig. 2H).

Neutrophils were activated, pro-inflammatory, and involved in leukocyte chemotaxis and activation on inflammation induction (Fig. 2H). The obvious decrease in the Augur score of neutrophils on day 10 indicated that neutrophils were gradually returning to the initial inactive state in the later stage (Fig. 2G). T cells exhibited proliferation, activation, and differentiation (Supplementary Fig. S2D). The programs of Ras signal transduction, Wnt, Notch, and T cell receptor signaling pathways, autophagy, response to TGF-beta, steroid hormone stimulus, and BMP were also activated in T cells (Supplementary Fig. S2D). NK cell-specific peaks were linked to genes associated with T cell activation and differentiation, Wnt signaling pathway, glycoprotein metabolic process, NF-kappaB signaling, and histone modification (Supplementary Fig. S2D).

To nominate the distal regulatory elements that dictate distinct biological states of these immune cell types, we constructed co-accessibility networks using the Cicero algorithm to infer cis-regulatory chromatin interactions. We found that the promoters of some key genes were highly accessible and interacted with distal regulatory elements in corresponding immune cell types, accounting for their specific expression. For example, the promoter of neutrophil- and MP-specific Thbs1, which regulates macrophage polarization and neutrophil infiltration, was active and established two long-range interactions with upstream putative enhancers (Fig. 2I). Neutrophils and MPs also exhibited specific expression and promoter-enhancer interactions at the chemokine Ccl3 and Cxcl2 loci (Supplementary Fig. S2E). The immunoregulatory receptor Trem3 was exclusively expressed in neutrophils, whereas Trem2 was specifically expressed in MPs. Trem2 plays a key role in suppressing inflammation and promoting phagocytosis in MPs. Their promoters were open and linked to downstream regulatory elements in a cell-type-specific manner (Fig. 2I). We also observed cell-type-specific regulatory elements that drove the expression of marker genes Il2rb and Itk in T and NK cells (Supplementary Fig. S2E).

We next determined whether there were differences between day 5 and day 10 for each immune cell type. As expected, a cohort of up-regulated and down-regulated genes was identified in each cell types (Fig. 2J). However, only reduced chromatin accessibility was observed at day 10 (Supplementary Fig. S2F). Neutrophils showed diminished expression of genes related to migration, activation, pro-inflammation and phagocytosis at day 10 (Supplementary Fig. S2G), such as Fcer1g, S100a8, S100a9, Ilb, Ccl3, Cxcl2 and Ccl4 (Fig. 2J). The Gene Ontology terms of cell killing, leukocyte chemotaxis, leukocyte mediated cytotoxicity and response to interferon-gamma were enriched in the down-reugulated gene cohorts of NK and T cells (Supplementary Fig. S2G). The expression of H2-K1, H2-D1, H2-Q7, Hspa8 and B2m, which are related to MHC I antigen presentation, was decreased at day 10 in T cells (Fig. 2J). In addition, the genes involved in antigen presentation, development, survival and homeostasis maintenance of NK cells, such as H2-K1, H2-Q7, H2-D1, H2-Q6, Il2rb, Id2, Tyrobp and Klre1, were also declined at day 10 (Fig. 2J; Supplementary Fig. S2G). These results suggested that the inflammatory response gradually subsides in the later stage.
Transcription Factor Regulatory Networks in Neutrophils and T Cells and NK Cells

It has been well established that transcription factors dictate cellular fate, function and physiological status. We applied SCENIC to construct transcription factor regulon networks for inferring master regulators across all immune cell types. We identified 146 regulons, some of which were commonly shared among multiple cell types, and some were cell-type specific. The top regulons for neutrophils were their markers CEBPE, CEBPD, EGR1, KLF2 and FOS (Figs. 3A, 3B), which were consistent with their expression levels and gene activities (Fig. 3C). CEBPD and FOS targeted the largest number of downstream genes (1101 and 866, respectively), with 331 of them being co-regulated by both transcription factors (Fig. 3D; Supplementary Fig. S3A). Notably, of the 127 neutrophil marker genes, 118 were targeted by one or more of these five transcription factors (Fig. 3D), highlighting their essential roles in neutrophil function.

Transcription factor regulatory network of neutrophils, T cells, and NK cells. (A) Ranked SCENIC transcription factor regulon activities in neutrophils, T cells, and NK cells inferred from scRNA-seq data. (B) Violin plots showing cell-type-specific SCENIC transcription factor regulon activities. (C) Dot plot showing expression and gene activity of selected cell-type-specific transcription factors. (D) Upset plot showing the size of overlaps between neutrophil markers and target genes of the indicated transcription factors. (E) Network plot showing target genes of the indicated transcription factors. (F) Genomic tracks showing chromatin accessibility around the indicated gene loci across all immune cell types. Peaks and peak-to-gene links are indicated below the tracks. (G) Heatmap showing the differential ChromVAR motif activities caclulated from scATAC-seq data between the indicated immune cell types. (H) Transcription factor footprinting inferred from chromatin accessibility for CEBPE, CEBPD, RUNX3, and ETS1 across all immune cell type.

The regulon scores, expressions and gene activities of SOX13 and IRF4 were highly specific for T cells (Figs. 3A-C). SOX13 and IRF4, crucial for T cell, regulated a cohort of genes associated with T cell survival, activation, differentiation, migration and function inhibition, such as Il7r, Ctla4, Tnfrsf10b, Havcr2, Jaml, Ltb4r1, Socs2, and Fam83a (Fig. 3E). IRF4 modulated the expression of Sox13. Tbx21 and Tcf7 exclusively expressed and epigenetically activated in NK cells were nominated as NK cell-specific transcription factors (Figs. 3A-C). TBX21 activated Il2rb (Fig. 3E), which is known to serve as a necessary signaling hub that regulates the proliferation, survival, metabolism, and effector functions of NK cells. Other genes associated with survival, differentiation and cellular killing of NK cells including Nkg7, Ncr1, Klrk1, Klra4, Klrag, Klra7, Cd160, Hcst, Myb, and Ets1 were also regulated by TBX21 or TCF7. TBX21 and TCF7 could self-regulate. The additional identification of ELK4 indicated that it may have a role in NK cells (Figs. 3A-C). We also observed that T and NK cells displayed a high degree of similarity in their molecular signatures, as evidenced by the consistent expression patterns, gene activities and regulon activities of ZEB1, LEF1, IKZF2, IKZF3, and ETS1 (Figs. 3A-C). They modulated a cohort of cell-type-specific functional genes (Supplementary Fig. S3B). All of these transcription factors mentioned above exhibited cell-type-specific accessible peaks at their promoters or within their loci (Fig. 3F; Supplementary Fig. S3C). Their promoters also interacted with one or more distal regulatory elements (Fig. 3F; Supplementary Fig. S3C).

We used chromVAR to compute transcription factor motif variability in open chromatin regions of each cell, identifying a cohort of transcription factors driving changes in chromatin accessibility in different immune cell types (Fig. 3G). We found that JUN, FOS, CEBPD and CEBPE exhibited high motif activity in neutrophils. The motifs of RORA and FLI1 were accessible in T cells. The open chromatin regions of NK cells were preferentially occupied by the ETS family of transcription factors and RUNX3. RUNX3 is known to regulate development, differentiation and cytotoxicity of NK cells. Transcription factor footprinting analysis further confirmed the proper binding of these cell-type-specific transcription factors (Fig. 3H; Supplementary Fig. S3D). We also found that NF-kappaB was activated in all immune cell types (Supplementary Figs. S3D, S3E). Together, our findings highlighted pivotal regulators of each distinct immune cell population.
Dynamics of MHC-II+ and MHC-II- MPs in Inflamed Cornea

Considering the potential role of MPs in tissue injury based on the above observation, we subsequently explored the molecular dynamics of MHC-II+CD74+ and MHC-II-CD93+CD84+STAB1+ MPs in corneal inflammation. We found that both MP populations expressed a cohort of genes associated with inflammation (Il1b, Saa3 and Ninj1), chemotaxis (Ccl3 and Ccl4) and phagocytosis-related lysosomal degradation (Lamp1, Ctsb, Ctsd, Ctsl, Ctsz and Atp6v0c) (Supplementary Fig. S4A). CUX1 and ETV6 exhibited exclusive expression and regulon activity in these MPs (Fig. 4B; Supplementary Fig. S4A), suggestive of their potential roles in MPs. S100a4, Cytip, Crip1, Lsp1 and Bhlhe40, which regulate MP migration, polarization and inflammatory response, exhibited higher expression levels and gene activities in MHC-II+ MPs (Fig. 4A). BHLHE40, BCL11A and NR4A2 were identified as key regulators of MHC-II+ MPs, as evidenced by their specific regulon activities (Fig. 4B). BCL11A directly activated those MHC-II moleculars, while NR4A2 regulated Cd74, a molecular chaperone of MHC-II (Fig. 4C).

Detailed transcriptional and epigenetic characteristics of MHC-II- and MHC-II+ MPs. (A) Violin plots showing the selected differentially expressed genes between MHC-II- and MHC-II+ MPs. (B) Dot plot showing SCENIC regulon activities of the indicated transcription factors across all immune cell types. (C) Network plot showing target genes of the indicated transcription factors. (D) Radar plot showing the significantly enriched biological process terms activated by MHC-II- MPs by gene set enrichment analysis based on scRNA-seq data of all immune cells. NES, normalized enrichment score. (E) UMAP plots of scATAC-seq data showing ChromVAR motif activities of Mafb, Mitf, and Maf in immune cell populations. (F) Transcription factor footprinting inferred from chromatin accessibility for MAFB, MITF and MAF in MHC-II- MPs. (G) Genomic tracks showing chromatin accessibility around Mafb locus across all immune cell types. Peaks and peak-to-gene links are indicated below the tracks. (H) Volcano plots showing the differentially expressed genes (scRNA-seq) between day 5 and day 10 after LPS treatment, respectively, in MHC-II- and MHC-II+ MPs.

Gene set enrichment analysis showed that compared with other immune cells, MHC-II- MPs had higher expression levels of genes associated with wound healing, cytokine production, innate immune response, defense response, immune effector process, apoptotic signaling pathways, proteolysis, endocytosis, macroautophagy, cell motibility, cell cycle and lipid metabolic process (Fig. 4D; Supplementary Fig. S4B). The genes encoding complement system (C1qa, C1qb, C1qc, C3ar1 and C5ar1), immunoreceptors (Cd38 and Trem2) and cytokines (Ccl2, Ccl7 and Pf4) were preferentially expressed and epigenetically activated in MHC-II- MPs (Fig. 4A; Supplementary Fig. S4C). These complement genes are known to regulate phagocytosis and inflammation balance. Compared to MHC-II+ MPs, MHC-II- MPs also exhibited higher expression levels and chromatin accessibility of genes that were involved in MP typical functions, such as lysosomal degradation (Atp6v1c1 and Atp6v1a), lipid metabolism (Abca1 and Plin2) and antisepsis (Slc11a1). Remarkably, Mafb, Maf, and Mitf, three critical anti-inflammatory and MP differentiation regulators, along with the anti-inflammatory genes Mdfic, Timp2, and Hmox1, were primarily expressed in MHC-II- MPs, consistent with their chromatin epigenetic state (Fig. 4A; Supplementary Fig. S4C). MHC-II- MP markers CD93 and STAB1 are also key anti-inflammatory receptors, whereas CD84 is a key pro-inflammatory immunoreceptor that mediates MP-lymphocyte interactions. Thus MHC-II- MPs possessed both pro- and anti-inflammatory properties simultaneously. MAFB, MAF and MITF exhibited the exclusive regulon activity, motif accessibility and footprinting signal flanking their motifs in MHC-II- MPs (Figs. 4B, 4E, 4F), highlighting their important regulatory roles in anti-inflammation gene. We also observed that Stab1, Lyz2 (antimicrobial lysozyme), Lmo2 (MP development), Sirpa (phagocytosis inhibition) and complement gene C1qc and C1qb were directly targeted by MAFB (Fig. 4C). Mafb was regulated by an upstream enhancer (Fig. 4G). MITF reuglated Ccl2, lipid metabolism gene Osbpl8 and immunoreceptor Fcrls (Fig. 4C). These data showed that MAFB, MAF and MITF were pivotal regulators of MHC-II- MPs.

These two MP subclusters changed significantly between day 5 and day 10 post-injury, as supported by the differentially expressed genes (Fig. 4H). SAA3 and IL-1beta are critical inflammatory amplifiers that recruit and activate diverse immune cell populations. The expression of Il1b was high at both time points in MHC-II+ MPs but declined at day 10 in MHC-II- MPs (Supplementary Fig. S4D). Saa3 exhibited the most significant downregulation in both MP types at day 10 (Fig. 4H). In MHC-II+ MPs, the pro-inflammatory genes Dock10, Pde4b, Gab2, Alcam, Nfkb1 and Rel were activated, but genes encoding the core components of ATP energy metabolism were down-regulated at day 10 (Fig. 4H). In the MHC-II- MPs, some pro-inflammatory regulators, including Dock10, Pde4b, Gab2, Nfkb1, Rel, Cebpb, C3ar1, C5ar1, Ccl2, and Ccl7, were upregulated, whereas another cohort of pro-inflammatory genes, such as Il1b, Saa3, Nlrp3, Fcgr4, Cxcl2, Ccl3, and Ccl4, were suppressed at day 10 (Fig. 4H). Some anti-inflammatory genes were also upregulated or downregulated, as evidenced by Sik3, Ptprj, Mdfic, Trem2, Timp2, and Hmox1. The reduction in the expression of the lysosome-related genes (Ctsd, Atp6v0c, Atp6v1e1, Atp6v1f, and Lamp1) involved in phagocytosis were also observed. Gene ontology analysis showed that the downregulated gene set in MHC-II- MPs was enriched for pro-inflammation terms including neutrophil migration, TNF and Il1b production and positive regulation of cytokine production (Supplementary Fig. S4E), which explained neutrophil reduction and inflammation resolution in the later stage of injury. In addition, the expression of genes related to wound healing, MP migration, and activation of T and B cells were upregulated at day 10 in MHC-II- MPs. In contrast, the genes associated with apoptosis, response to oxidative stress, phagocytosis, autophagy and lipid and ATP metabolism were downregulated (Supplementary Fig. S4E). Together, these findings highlighted that MHC-II+ MPs were proinflammatory and MHC-II- MPs possessed dual pro- and anti-inflammatory properties but exhibited diminished capacity for phagocytosis, apoptosis, and energy metabolism, reflecting the complexity of inflammatory regulation.
Inflammation Causes Dysfunction of the Corneal Epithelial Lineage

Although numerous studies have sought to reveal the gene expression patterns of distinct corneal epithelial cell types, their epigenetic landscape remains largely unexplored. We found that LSC markers Gpha2, Ifitm3, and p63, as well as the cell proliferation marker Ki67, were epigenetically active in LSCs and TACs (Fig. 5A; Supplementary Fig. S5A). LSCs and TACs showed high motif activity of p63 and footprinting signals around p63 binding motifs (Fig. 5B). Muc4, a marker of the terminally differentiated corneal superficial layer, opened its chromatin exclusively in the later-differentiated corneal suprabasal-3 and superficial clusters (Supplementary Fig. S5A). The high motif activity and footprint signal of EHF and ELF3 in corneal suprabasal-3 and superficial clusters highlighted their potential regulatory role in corneal epithelial differentiation (Fig. 5B; Supplementary Fig. S5B). Interestingly, the promoter of the corneal epithelial marker Krt12 and its interacting enhancer were both open in all epithelial cell types (Fig. 5A). This pre-accessible chromatin state at the stem cell stage primed for its rapid expression upon differentiation. As expected, the loci of Pax6, Runx1, Smad3, and Foxc1, the well-known corneal epithelial lineage fate determinators, exhibited high accessibility in all CEC types (Supplementary Fig. S5A). High-frequency chromatin interactions also occurred within their loci to ensure their proper expression.

Molecular dynamics of corneal epithelial lineage induced by inflammation. (A) Genomic tracks showing chromatin accessibility around the indicated gene loci across the indicated cell types. Peaks and peak-to-gene links are indicated below the tracks. (B) Transcription factor footprinting inferred from chromatin accessibility for p63, Ehf, and Elf3 in corneal epithelial lineage. (C) ScRNA expression of Stat3 across the indicated cell types in the indicated groups. (D) UMAP plots of scRNA-seq showing the expression of the indicated genes in corneal epithelial lineage. (E) Heatmap showing the enriched gene ontology terms in LSCs in the indicated groups based on scRNA-seq data. (F) Heatmap showing the differential ChromVAR motif activities between LSCs in the indicated groups.

Differential accessibility analysis showed that a cohort of peaks increased chromatin accessibility on day 5 after LPS treatment in the epithelial lineage, but they almost all recovered to normal levels by day 10 (Supplementary Fig. S5C). The inflammatory microenvironment mainly led to a reduction in chromatin accessibility of the fibroblast lineage at both time points. Some peaks with reduced chromatin accessibility were observed in the epithelial lineage at both time points. We also found that inflammation induced changes in the expression of numerous genes in all corneal and limbal cell types (Supplementary Fig. S5C). The key pro-inflammatory regulators Stat3 exhibited increased expression in LSCs, TACs and CECs on days 10 or 5 (Fig. 5C; Supplementary Fig. S5D). The corneal epithelial differentiation program was disrupted, as evidenced by reduce in the differentiation markers Aqp5, Slurp1, and Lypd2 but not Muc4 in some CECs and complete loss of KRT12, CLU, and ALDH3A1 proteins (Figs. 1A, 5D).

To further reveal the pathological change of LSCs, we identified the differential biological processes induced by inflammation (Fig. 5E). The metabolic pathways of pyruvate, galactose, glycerolipid, glycolysis and gluconeogenesis were upregulated at day 5. The genes associated with cell cycle, ErbB and insulin signaling pathways were upregulated at day 10. The genes involved in mTOR, JAK-STAT, p53 pathways, and DNA replication were upregulated on both time points. Inflammation stimulation promoted LSC proliferation, which was further confirmed by the increased expressions and motif activities of CEBPD and p53 (Fig. 5F). The increased motif activities of NF-kappaB and Stat1:Stat2 highlighted the inflammation-featured state of LSCs (Fig. 5F). In addition, inflammation inhibited genes related to gap junction, adherens junction, and Wnt and calcium pathways, all of which are important to LSCs (Fig. 5E). TEAD proteins are typical partners of YAP1, which is important to maintain stemness and injury repair of LSCs. The decreased motif accessibility of TEAD 1/2/3/4 was also observed in LSCs (Fig. 5F). Together, inflammation caused LSC exhaustion, leading to corneal epithelial dysfunction.
Cell-Cell Signaling Communication Networks Under Acute Inflammation

To uncover how the inflammatory niche affected the corneal epithelium, the CellChat tool was applied to identify the underlying immune-epithelial interaction networks. We observed frequent and robust interactions between immune cell types and the limbal-corneal compartments (Fig. 6A). Overall, MHC-II+ MPs and neutrophils were preferred as signal receivers, whereas LSC and TACs-2 populations mainly acted as signal emitters (Fig. 6B). MHC-II- MPs exhibited comparably high incoming and outgoing interaction strength (Fig. 6B). Specifically, epithelial cells, as well as immune cells, secreted CCL and CXCL chemokine signals to crosstalk with immune cells (Fig. 6C). Neutrophils, NK cells, T cells and all epithelial cells secreted MIF to activate MPs. Neutrophil and MPs were the primary receivers of inflammatory-associated Annexin signal derived from epithelial cells. LSCs and TACs emitted pro-proliferative PTN signal to regulate themselves and all other cell types. Of note, we found that neutrophils and MPs secreted VEGF signal to induce neovascularization (Fig. 6C).

Cell-cell interaction networks in the inflamed limbal-corneal tissues. (A) CellChat interaction networks across all epithelial and immune cell types based on scRNA-seq data. (B) The cell types showing the incoming and outgoing interaction strength of total signaling. (C) Chord plots showing the sender and receivers of the indicated signalings.
Discussion

Tissue homeostasis and regeneration require proper immune microenvironment. As an immune-privileged tissue, the cornea is highly sensitive to disordered inflammatory microenvironment, which positions the cornea as a tractable model for decoding immune-stem cell crosstalk in tissue pathology. Our comprehensive single-cell transcriptomic and epigenomic analysis revealed a sophisticated molecular framework through which aberrant immune-epithelial stem cell crosstalk derived pathological corneal regeneration. We demonstrated that inflammatory injury profoundly reprogramed both epithelial differentiation programs and immune cell functionality. We observed extensive intercellular communication between immune cells and epithelial cells. These findings provided fundamental insights into the mechanisms underlying inflammation-mediated tissue pathology.

The corneal immune-privileged status is essential for maintaining optical clarity. On injury, this privilege is rapidly revoked: neutrophils surge within hours, followed by infiltration of macrophages, dendritic cells, T cells, and NK cells. Neutrophils secrete IL-1alpha/IL-1beta to amplify inflammation and recruite other immune cells and eliminate pathogens via phagocytosis, reactive oxygen species, degranulation and neutrophil extracellular traps. Consistently, extensive neutrophil infiltration was observed on day 5 after LPS treatment, but significantly decreased by day 10. These infiltrating neutrophils exhibited capacity for pro-inflammation, phagocytosis and degranulation. The genes encoding cytokines and chemokines were expressed and epigenetically activated in neutrophils on day 5, but were silenced by day 10, suggesting their pioneering role in the early stage. Recent intravital two-photon and confocal microscopy studies reveal that small numbers of CD3+ T cells are constitutively present in both the human and murine cornea. They contribute to corneal epithelial homeostasis and wound healing. In chronic inflammatory context, such as diabetic keratopathy, corneal T cells exhibit sustained cytotoxic signatures. We found that T cells in inflamed cornea were characterized by proliferation, migration, activation and differentiation and reduced their cytotoxicity and energy metabolism in the later stage of inflammation.

passages.text: In the naive state, the corneal stroma contains resident immune cells, predominantly MPs that serve as sentinels for pathogen detection and tissue homeostasis. These resident MPs exhibit an anti-inflammatory phenotype and contribute to immune tolerance. A central insight is the functional diversification of MPs in the inflammation response. we defined two distinct subpopulations of MPs, characterized by MHC-II+ and MHC-II-Cd93+Cd84+Stab1+. Classical macrophage polarization theory partitions cells into pro-inflammatory M1 or anti-inflammatory M2 subsets. MHC-II- MPs acquired a hybrid state of pro- and ant-inflammation with a unique transcriptional and epigeneitic signature defined by MAF, MAFB and MITF, consistent with the view that MP polarization exists on a spectrum rather than as binary M1/M2 states. MHC-II- MPs exhibited pro- and anti-inflammatory features and reduced phagocytic, lysosomal and metabolic signatures, which explained a shift from early antimicrobial and phagocytic functions to tissue remodeling and neutrophil resolution. Our identification of MHC-II- MPs expands the paradigm of MP plasticity in corneal inflammation. This hybrid phenotype aligns with emerging concepts of MP functional plasticity and heterogeneity in tissue repair.

Our findings establish a direct link between molecular dysregulation and corneal pathology. The observed arrest of LSCs in a hyperproliferative but differentiation-blocked state explains delayed wound healing. Furthermore, the repression of Wnt signaling and reduced chromatin accessibility of TEAD motifs likely compromise epithelial adhesion and migration, driving persistent epithelial defects. Notably, while inflammation subsided by day 10, the chromatin landscape of immune cells remained primed. This "epigenetic memory" suggests a latent mechanism for chronic scarring or recurrent inflammation even after clinical resolution. Targeting these specific epigenetic and signaling bottlenecks offers a new therapeutic avenue for restoring corneal integrity.

passages.text: Effects of dietary palygorskite supplementation on production performance and reproductive function of laying hens

Oxidative stress reduces the production performance of laying hens by impairing their reproductive system. Palygorskite (Pal), a fibrous clay mineral, exhibits antioxidant properties; however, its effects on production performance and reproductive function of laying hens remain unknown. The aim of this study was to determine the effects of dietary Pal supplementation on production performance and reproductive function of laying hens. A total of 256 laying hens were divided into two groups: the control group, which was fed a basal diet, and the Pal group, which was fed a basal diet supplemented with Pal. The production performance, gonadal development, reproductive hormone levels, antioxidant capacity, and metabolomic and transcriptome profiles of the two groups were compared. Compared to those in the control group, the average daily egg production, eggshell thickness, oviduct weight, oviduct index, and the levels of luteinizing hormone, progesterone, and follicle-stimulating hormone were significantly higher in the Pal group. Following Pal treatment, the total antioxidant capacity and total superoxide dismutase activities as well as glutathione levels in the serum increased, whereas malondialdehyde levels in the ovary and eggshell gland decreased. Moreover, upregulated expression levels of antioxidant genes, such as catalase, superoxide dismutase 1, superoxide dismutase 2, and NAD(P)H quinone dehydrogenase 1, as well as downregulated expression levels of pro-inflammatory factors, such as tumor necrosis factor-alpha were observed following Pal supplementation. Furthermore, metabolomics analysis revealed that the levels of metabolites such as ritonavir, nicotinate riboside, and inosine were upregulated in the Pal group. Similarly, transcriptome profiling revealed that the expression levels of genes involved in the anti-inflammatory response, follicular development, egg production, and eggshell quality were upregulated in the Pal group. These findings indicated that dietary Pal supplementation enhanced the production performance, antioxidant capacity, anti-inflammatory response, and reproductive function of laying hens. Therefore, these findings lay the foundation for the development of strategies and protocols for the inclusion of Pal in the diet of laying hens.
Introduction

Egg-laying efficiency is influenced by various factors, including nutrition, feeding management, breed, and reproductive health. A properly functioning reproductive system is of utmost importance for maintaining high egg production rates. When an excess of free radicals induces oxidative stress, which in turn disrupts the hormonal secretion and reproductive function of laying hens. Specifically, this can damage the ovary and oviduct, resulting in blocked follicular development, a reduced egg production rate, and poor egg quality. Thus, to ensure high production efficiency in laying hens, the balance between oxidation and antioxidation should be maintained. Dietary supplementation with antioxidant compounds, such as Vitamin E, organic selenium, and plant extracts, is an effective strategy for alleviating oxidative damage to the reproductive system.

Fibrous clays can also mitigate oxidative stress and cell damage, and have been reported to inhibit lipid peroxidation effectively. Palygorskite (Pal), also known as attapulgite, is chemically categorized as hydrated magnesium aluminum silicate. It is a fibrous clay mineral with a crystalline structure composed of 2:1 phyllosilicate ribbon, consisting of micropores, channels, and abundant reactive -OH groups. These structural attributes impart Pal with distinctive properties, including a large specific surface area, high porosity, excellent ion-exchange and adsorption capacities, and favorable colloidal properties. Owing to its unique properties, Pal is widely used in chemical, environmental, and pharmaceutical industries. Previous studies have demonstrated multifaceted benefits of dietary Pal supplementation in laying hens. For example, reported improvements in digestive function and intestinal morphology, which may contribute to laying performance and egg quality. demonstrated that Pal improves the growth performance of broilers by enhancing intestinal flora.

Pal is typically composed of aggregated rod-crystal bundles. The dissociation of these bundles improves the function of Pal. For example, the bundle-dissociated form of Pal exhibits enhanced antioxidant efficacy and growth-promoting effects. In addition to improving growth performance, it also alleviated inflammation and intestinal mucosal barrier damage in broilers challenged with Escherichia coli. However, to the best of our knowledge, the effects of bundle-dissociated Pal on the production performance and reproductive function of laying hens have not yet been investigated.

The objective of this study is to determine whether bundle-dissociated Pal exerts beneficial effects on the reproductive system health of laying hens through its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects, and enhanced production performance and egg quality in commercial laying hens.
Materials and methods
Experimental materials

Pal was procured from Jiangsu Jinhan New Materials (Jiangsu, China). The raw material was subjected to ultrasound-assisted crystal bundle dissociation prior to use. The main chemical components of the processed Pal were SiO2 (60.91%), Al2O3 (11.84%), Fe2O3 (9.84%), MgO (7.79%), CaO (4.22%), K2O (2.08%), TiO2 (1.31%), and P2O5 (1.15%), which were measured using an Epsilon 3 X-ray fluorescence spectrometer (PANalytical B.V. Almelo, Netherlands).

The Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Nanjing Agricultural University approved all the animal experiments performed in this study. A total of 256 Hy-Line Gray laying hens (74 weeks old) were randomly assigned to two groups, each with eight replicates of 16 hens: the control group, which was fed a basal diet; and the Pal group, which was fed a basal diet supplemented with 5 g/kg of Pal. The formulation and nutritional composition of the basal diet are shown in Table 1.

This experiment was conducted in a commercial laying hen facility (Panchu, Nanjing, China) equipped with a battery cage system. A cage (603 mm x 640 mm x 450/380 mm) raised eight laying hens and equipped with three nipple drinkers and a U-shaped feed trough (603 mm x 140 mm x 90 mm). The middle and bottom tiers were used, with two adjacent cages in the same column serving as a replicate. A 16L:8D photoperiod (lights on at 06:00 and off at 22:00) was maintained throughout the trial. Feed and water were provided ad libitum, with hens were fed twice daily at 08:00 and 16:00. The facility was equipped with a negative-pressure longitudinal mechanical ventilation system. Throughout the study, the house temperature was maintained at 20-25 C.

The experimental lasted for ten weeks, including a 2-week preliminary experiment and an 8-week formal trial (from 74 to 84 weeks old). At the end of the experiment, one laying hen with a body weight similar to the average body weight was randomly selected from each replicate, with a total of eight hens per group, for tissue and blood sample collection.

Blood was drawn from the wing vein and centrifuged at 3,500 r/min for 10 min at 4  C. The collected serum was kept at -80  C for subsequent analysis. After blood collection, the hens were euthanized via cervical dislocation. The liver, ovary, and eggshell gland were aseptically collected, snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at -80  C. The abdominal cavity was rapidly opened, and the cecal was resected and placed on a tray.
Measurement indicators and methods

Productive Performance and Egg Quality. The number of eggs, total egg weight were determined daily. Feed intake was recorded weekly. The egg production rate (%) was calculated by dividing the number of eggs laid per day by the number of live hens per day x 100. Average daily egg production (g) was calculated using the following equation: daily egg production x egg weight (g). The feed conversion rate (FCR) was calculated using the following formula: FCR=feed intake (g)/egg weight (g).

At weeks four and eight of the formal trial, three eggs were collected from each replicate for quality assessment. A total of 24 eggs were obtained from each group and used to examine egg weight, albumen height, yolk color, Haugh unit, shell strength, and shell thickness. Eggshell strength was measured using an eggshell strength meter (Model-II; Robotmation, Tokyo, Japan). Eggshell thickness was determined by taking the average eggshell thickness at the sharp end, blunt end, and middle part of the egg, which were measured using a micrometer. Egg weight, albumen height, Haugh unit, and yolk color were analyzed using an egg quality tester (EMT-5200; Robotmation, Tokyo, Japan).

Gonad Organ Index and Follicle Development Grade. After follicle removal, the fallopian tubes and ovaries were weighed, and the fallopian tube length was measured (accurate to 0.01 mm). The follicles were graded and counted according to the method described by. The gonad organ index was calculated using the following equation:

Serum Reproductive Hormone Levels. The serum levels of estradiol (E2), luteinizing hormone (LH), progesterone (P4), and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) were determined using ELISA kits (Hong Sheng, Nanjing, China), according to the manufacturer's instructions.

Antioxidant Capacity of the Serum, Ovary, and Eggshell Gland. The malondialdehyde (MDA) levels in the serum, ovary, and eggshell gland samples were determined using the thiobarbituric acid method. The total superoxide dismutase (T-SOD) and total antioxidant capacity (T-AOC) activities were measured using the hydroxylamine and 2,2'-azinobis-(3-ethylbenzthiazoline-6-sulphonate) methods, respectively. Catalase (CAT) activity and glutathione (GSH) levels were determined using the colorimetric method. CAT, T-SOD, and T-AOC activities per milligram of protein in the serum, ovary, and eggshell gland samples were calculated. The manufacturer's instructions provided in the kits purchased from Nanjing Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute (Nanjing, China) were followed to perform the aforementioned methods.

Detection of Ig Content and Inflammatory Factor Levels. The serum levels of secretory IgA (sIgA), IgG, IgM, tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha), interferon-gamma (INF-gamma), IL-1beta, IL-4, and IL-10 were determined using ELISA kits (Hong Sheng, Nanjing, China), following the manufacturer's instructions.
Omics technologies

Metabolomics Analysis. Cecal contents were quickly removed and immediately frozen in liquid nitrogen or at -80  C to prevent metabolite degradation. The cecal samples were thawed on ice and homogenized at a low temperature (4  C, 60 Hz, for 2-5 min) in pre-chilled PBS or methanol/water (80% methanol). Afterwards, metabolites were extracted using an organic solvent method (e.g., a 2:2:1 v/v mixture of methanol/acetonitrile/water) by vortexing for 30 s and sonicating on ice for 10 min. The supernatant was collected after centrifugation (12,000 x g, 4  C, for 15 min) and filtered through a 0.22-mum filter to remove proteins and impurities, if necessary. Quality control samples were prepared to monitor system stability. Isotopic internal standards were added to correct for signal drift. The processed samples were stored at -80  C.

A liquid chromatography-quadrupole time-of-flight tandem mass spectrometry system was employed for metabolomic analysis. Chromatographic separation was achieved using a Waters Acquity UPLC HSS T3 column (1.8 mum, 2.1 x 100 mm). The mobile phase consisted of 0.1% formic acid (solvent A) and acetonitrile (solvent B) at a 0.35 mL/min flow rate. The chromatographic separation was performed using a 10 muL injection volume at a column temperature of 40  C. The elution started with an isocratic step with 50.0% solvent B for 3 min. Prior to the analysis, mobile phase A was vacuum-filtered through a 0.45-mum cellulose nitrate membrane. All samples were maintained at 4  C in an autosampler, with acetonitrile as the needle rinse solution. For mass spectrometric detection, a TurboIonSpray source was operated in both positive and negative ion modes with multiple-reaction monitoring. The source conditions were set as follows: source temperature, 550  C; ion source gas 1 and 2, 55 psi each; ion spray voltage, 5,500 V; curtain gas, 35 psi; and collision gas, medium. The analyte and the internal standard (tolbutamide) were monitored under these conditions.

The raw dataset was converted to the mzxl format using massconvert and dataset was then processed using Tidymass software. The raw data were processed through a series of procedures, including peak alignment, feature extraction, normalization, and retention time correction. Following data acquisition, raw liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry data were processed through a pipeline consisting of peak detection, alignment, filtering, and feature characterization. This procedure, aided by a statistical comparison component, generated a comprehensive data matrix containing sample information, metabolite peak names, retention times, m/z values, and signal intensities. Initial metabolite characterization was conducted by querying the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) and Human Metabolome Database. Metabolite identity was confirmed by evaluating the precise m/z, secondary fragments, and isotope distribution.

Total RNA Extraction, cDNA Library Preparation, and Sequencing. Transcriptome analysis was performed on the ovary and eggshell gland samples from both groups. Total RNA was extracted from the ovary and eggshell gland samples using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA), according to the manufacturer's instructions. Total RNA quality was assessed on agarose gels and quantified spectrophotometrically (NanoDrop ND-2000; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). The RNA-seq library was constructed using a TruSeq Stranded mRNA Library Prep Kit (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA) and sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Shanghai, China). Adapter and low-quality sequences were removed from the raw data using FastQC, and clean reads were aligned to the Gallus gallus genome (GRCg6a) using Bowtie2/TopHat2.

Bioinformatic Analysis of Differentially Expressed Genes (DEGs). Gene expression level was quantified using fragments per kilobase of transcript per million mapped fragments (FPKM). Reads were mapped to a non-redundant transcript set, and the genes with FPKM > 1 were considered expressed. Differential expression was analyzed using the DESeq package. The DEGs with llog2 fold changel > 1 and P < 0.05 were considered significant. The DEGs were subjected to Gene Ontology and KEGG analyses.

passages.text: Statistical analysis

Differential metabolic features between the Pal and control groups were identified by performing principal component analysis (PCA) and orthogonal partial least squares-discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA). Differentially expressed metabolites (DEMs) were screened based on variable importance in projection values > 1 from the OPLS-DA model and P-values < 0.05 resulting from two-tailed Student's t-test, rendering metabolite identification with high group-discriminating power and statistical significance. Pathway analysis of the identified DEMs was performed using MetaboAnalyst 5.0 (https://www.metaboanalyst.ca/) and by referring to the KEGG online database (https://www.keggjp/).

The data were processed preliminarily in Microsoft Excel 2016 and then subjected to SPSS 26.0. Significant differences between the groups were analyzed by independent samples t-test. Prior to the t-test, homogeneity of variance was assessed using the Levene's test. If variances were equal, Student's t-test was applied; otherwise, Welch's t-test was used. Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05. The data are expressed as the mean +- standard error of the mean.
